Explanation:

In India, only specific magistrates can order exhumation:

  • First Class, District, Sub-Divisional, Executive Magistrates.
  • Law enforcement cannot order exhumation independently.

Exhumation
  • Legal disinterment of a previously buried body
  • Conducted when post-burial examination is necessary
  • Under Section 196(4) of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (which replaces Section 176 of the CrPC), provisions relating to inquest and exhumation empower the Executive Magistrate to order exhumation when necessary.

Common Reasons
  • Criminal Cases:
    • Re-examine suspected homicides disguised as suicides/accidents.
    • Investigate deaths from criminal abortion or negligence.
    • Retrieve evidence (e.g., bullets).
  • Civil Cases:
    • Insurance/worker's compensation claims.
    • Professional negligence cases.
    • Inheritance disputes or identity verification.
    • Correct burial errors (If the wrong body was buried)

Procedure Requirements
  • Timing & Personnel:
    • Must be conducted during daylight (start in the morning).
    • A medical officer, magistrate, and police officer are required.
  • Documentation:
    • Verify grave location and markers.
    • Collect soil samples (above, below, and beside the body/coffin).
    • Document body position and appearance.
    • Create a detailed grave diagram.
    • Photograph grave, coffin, and body.

Handling Guidelines
  • Avoid altering the body (no use of disinfectants or pesticides).
  • Use plank or plastic sheet for removal if decomposition is minimal.
  • Transport the body to the mortuary for post-mortem examination.


Reference:

Goutam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd Edition, Pages 119, 120

Explanation:

  • In forensic autopsies, the stomach is usually opened along the greater curvature to minimize disruption of stomach anatomy and allows the pathologist to collect and examine the stomach contents effectively, which is critical in cases of suspected poisoning.

Procedure for Stomach Dissection:

  • Two ligatures are applied at the cardiac end of the esophagus and two ligatures are below the pyloric end of the stomach.
  • The stomach is removed by cutting between the double ligatures at both ends.
  • The stomach is then opened along the greater curvature.
  • The mucous membrane is examined for the presence of any stains, congestion, hemorrhage, desquamation, ulceration, sloughing, or perforation.
  • The contents of the stomach are noted with respect to quantity, nature of material/food, state of digestion, color, and smell.

The modified Y-shaped incision provides comprehensive exposure of the thoracic, abdominal, and neck organs, making it ideal for forensic cases requiring detailed neck examination.

  • It allows better cosmetic closure, reducing postmortem disfigurement and minimizing the risk of fluid leakage sometimes seen with the traditional Y-shaped incision.

  • Situations requiring a better cosmetic outcome
  • Non-forensic hospital autopsies


Y-shaped incision (Option B) exposes thoracic and abdominal organs but offers poor access to neck structures and may increase postmortem fluid leakage. Indications include:

  • Standard medicolegal autopsy
  • Suspicious or unnatural deaths
  • Cases requiring detailed thoracic organ examination
  • Cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal pathology evaluation


T-shaped incision (Option D), rarely used, a horizontal cut across the shoulders (bilateral acromion processes) and a vertical cut from the suprasternal notch down to the pubic symphysis. Indications include:

  • Selected forensic cases requiring enhanced chest wall exposure
  • Situations where a better cosmetic closure is desired than a Y-incision
  • Special institutional preference cases

An X-incision (or cruciate incision) in an autopsy is a specialised technique used primarily to examine the back of the body, often in cases of suspected torture or custodial death with injuries from blunt instruments. This technique involves cutting from the back of the shoulder (acromion) to the opposing hip (iliac crest) to assess for hidden subcutaneous haemorrhages.



Reference:
  1. Parikh's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 8th Edition, Page 107

In the Virchow method (by Rudolf Virchow), each organ is removed and examined individually, rather than removing all organs together as a single mass

Evisceration techniques in autopsy:

En Masse (Letulle)

(Option A ruled out)

 This is an "en masse" technique where the entire organ block (all thoracic and abdominal organs) is removed from the body as one single unit and then dissected.

Virchow’s Method

(Option D)

 This method involves the removal and dissection of organs one by one. This approach allows for a detailed examination of each organ.

In Situ Dissection (Rokitansky)

(Option B ruled out)

 This technique involves "in situ" dissection, where the organs are examined and dissected while still inside the body, with minimal or no removal.

En block (Ghon)

(Option C ruled out)

 This is an "en bloc" technique where the organs are removed in functional blocks (e.g., the thoracic block, the abdominal block, the urogenital block).

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Cherry red hypostasis

Explanation:

In this scenario, a family died in a closed room full of smoke from a wood fire, which likely caused carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Cherry-red post-mortem staining is a hallmark sign of carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning.

Postmortem Staining in Poisoning Cases

  • Postmortem staining (Livor mortis) is the skin discoloration after death due to blood settling in dependent areas.
  • The color of the staining can indicate certain types of poisoning:

Poison

Postmortem Staining Characteristics

Opium (Option C ruled out)

Purple or blackish staining

Carbon monoxide (Option A)

Cherry red discoloration (COHb > 30%)

Hydrogen sulfide

Greenish discoloration in tissues

Datura

Asphyxial signs (no specific color)

Organochlorine/Kerosene

Asphyxial signs (no specific color)

Phosphates, aniline, and nitrites (Option D ruled out)

Brown-colored pigmentation

Carbon Monoxide

Physical Appearance
  • Odourless, colorless, non-irritating gas, lighter than air

Sources of Poisoning
  • Incomplete combustion of almost of fuel (wood, charcoal, gas, kerosene)
  • Automobile exhaust
  • Fires: A common cause of accidental CO poisoning resulting in mass deaths - large building (hotel, theatre, block of flats, etc.) in flames
  • Paint remover (especially methylene chloride)
  • Tobacco smoke

Normal CO level in plasma
  • 1 to 5 %
  • 7 to 8 % in smokers

Mode of Action
  • 230 to 270 times greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen
  • Leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve
  • Reduced arterial oxygen content
  • Inactivating mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase - cellular respiration is interfered
  • CO-induced brain injuries are common in basal ganglia, cerebral white matter, hippocampus, and cerebellum.

Clinical Features
  • Depends on the concentration of CO in the blood
  • CO exposure during pregnancy is teratogenic

Diagnosis
  • Carboxyhemoglobin level (COHb) in blood
  • Arterial blood gases

Treatment
  • Oxygen (100%) through a tight-fitting mask or endotracheal tube, until COHb falls to 15 to 20%
  • Hyperbaric oxygen: Inhalation of oxygen at a pressure greater than 1 atmosphere absolute

Autopsy Findings
  • Cherry red (pink) color of skin, inner aspects of lips, nail beds, tongue, palms and soles
  • Cutaneous bullae (skin blisters) in the calves, buttocks, wrists, and knees
  • Cherry pink color of blood and tissues
  • Firmer white matter of the brain
  • Necrosis and cavitation of basal ganglia

Cyanosis (Option B) is not appreciated in CO poisoning.



Reference:

Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 539, 564, 587, 590, 602.
question: A family died in a closed room that was full of smoke from a wood fire. Which of the following findings is likely to be seen on the body?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: C) Arsenic

Explanation:

Among the options, arsenic is the poison that can be detected in visceral organs even if the person did not consume it immediately before death. This is because arsenic accumulates in body tissues over time due to its slow elimination and remains present in organs such as the liver and kidneys regardless of recent intake.

Morphine (Option A): Only present if recently ingested or administered; not naturally stored in organs.

Aconite (Option B): A plant toxin that appears in the body only after recent consumption.

Alcohol (Option D): Primarily detected only if recently consumed; endogenous amounts are negligible.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8840458

correctAnswer: B. To confirm the diaphragmatic position to avoid postmortem air artifact in the lungs
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In a fetal or neonatal autopsy, the abdomen is opened first and the diaphragm is checked by passing a finger before the thorax is opened to ensure that no air is accidentally introduced into the thoracic cavity.

  • Introducing air could falsely inflate the lungs and lead to an incorrect interpretation that the infant had breathed - creating a false-positive hydrostatic (lung-float) test.
  • This step is therefore critical when distinguishing live birth from stillbirth.

To accurately measure abdominal organ size (Option A): Organ measurements are not the reason for opening the abdomen first and can be done later in the autopsy.

To check for intra-abdominal hemorrhage before thoracic examination (Option C): Hemorrhage assessment is important but not the priority in determining live birth vs. stillbirth.

To evaluate gastrointestinal malformations early in the autopsy (Option D): GI malformation assessment does not influence lung aeration testing and is not why the abdomen is opened first.



Reference:

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) NaF

Explanation:

  • For toxic analysis, like in alcohol abuse, the ideal preservative for blood is sodium fluoride.
  • It inhibits glycolysis by blocking enolase
  • Prevents post-collection fall in glucose
  • Preserves alcohol concentration, making it essential in suspected alcohol poisoning

Various methods of preserving viscera:

  1. Saturated salt solution
  2. Formalin fixation
  3. Freezing
  4. Alcohol preservation
  5. Formaldehyde solution
  6. Formalin-alcohol solution
  7. Frozen section
  8. Liquid nitrogen

Specimens for Analysis

Specimen

Importance

Blood

Primary specimen; collect from femoral, iliac, or axillary veins to avoid contamination.

Preservative: Lithium heparin or EDTA tube, Sodium fluoride/oxalate (Option A), if alcohol is suspected

Urine

Useful for detecting parent compounds and metabolites of poisons.

Preservative: No preservative, sodium fluoride is added, if alcohol is

Suspected

Gastric Contents

Helps identify ingested poisons and their concentrations through vomitus and stomach contents analysis.

Preservative: Saturated salt solution if there is no chance of acid poison.(Option B)

Rectified spirit if poisoned by acid (Option C)

.

Liver

Analyzes metabolism and concentration of drugs; critical when blood/urine concentrations are low. Bile can detect specific substances like chlorpromazine and morphine.

Preservative: Saturated salt solution if there is no chance of acid poison.

Rectified spirit if poisoned by acid.

Hair and Nails

Detects heavy metal poisoning; metals accumulate in keratin. Neutron activation analysis identifies specific metals and exposure patterns.

Scene Residues

Provides clues about the poison through materials found at the scene, such as tablets or empty containers.

Formalin (Option C) is commonly used for general tissue preservation and fixation in anatomical pathology, but it is not specifically preferred for toxicology autopsy. It may affect the results of toxicological analyses.



Reference:

Goutam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd edition, page 114.
question: Blood during autopsy is preserved in?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Precipitin test

Explanation:

  • The test which can give the species differentiation is the precipitin test.
  • Precipitin tests can be done by extracting species-specific protein from bone into a solution and testing it against specific antisera of humans.
  • The techniques such as electrophoresis or gel diffusion can now identify human tissue.

Confirmatory Tests for Blood Stains in Forensic Medicine

  • Confirmatory tests are critical for identifying blood presence and origin in forensic investigations.
  • Methods include chemical, immunological, and mass spectrometry techniques for reliable results.

Chemical Confirmatory Tests

Test

Description

Takayama Test

[[figure-1]]

Detects hemoglobin by forming red, feathery crystals of pyridine ferroprotoporphyrin.

Teichmann Test (Option D ruled out)

[[figure-2]]

Converts hemoglobin to hemin, creating brownish-yellow rhomboid crystals, confirming blood presence.

Immunological Tests

Test

Description

Precipitin Test (Option A)

Identifies species origin through antibody-antigen reactions, using antisera specific to human blood.

HemaTrace Test

Uses monoclonal antibodies to detect human hemoglobin, showing a visible pink band for confirmation.

Mass Spectrometry Techniques

  • Thread Spray Mass Spectrometry: Analyzes whole blood directly on textiles, differentiating species based on lipid composition and hemoglobin chains. It offers high sensitivity and specificity.

Acid-phosphatase (Option B) This test can be used to detect seminal fluid.

LDH (Option C) cannot be used for species differentiation.



Reference:

Hydrostatic test/ Raygat's test/ Breslau's 1 life test/ Lung floatation test

  • If the baby had respired, the alveoli would be expanded/ dilated.

Explanation:

Aspect

Details

Introduction
  • Body packing refers to the illegal transport of narcotic drugs by swallowing or inserting sealed packets into body cavities
  • Commonly involves cocaine or heroin
  • Packets may be concealed in the stomach, intestine, rectum, or vagina

Complications
  • Gastrointestinal obstruction
  • Gastrointestinal haemorrhage
  • Rupture of packets causing fatal narcotic intoxication

Imaging
  • Abdominal X-ray is the first-line investigation
  • Ultrasound or CT scan may be used if the diagnosis is unclear

Management of an asymptomatic patient
  • Whole bowel irrigation may be done cautiously
  • Enemas may help the passage of packets
  • Food intake is avoided until all packets are expelled
  • Metoclopramide may be used to promote gastric emptying

Management of a symptomatic patient
  • Continuous naloxone infusion may be required in opioid toxicity
  • Whole bowel irrigation is performed
  • Surgical intervention may be needed in obstruction or packet rupture

Body stuffing (Option B): Body stuffing refers to hurried swallowing or concealment of small quantities of drugs to avoid police detection. The packets are poorly wrapped and therefore have a greater risk of rupture compared to body packing.

Body storage (Option C): The term “body storage” literally means storing something inside the body. However, it is not an accepted or recognised medicolegal terminology in forensic medicine for drug concealment.

Body masking (Option D): The word “masking” means hiding or concealing something. Although the term suggests concealment, “body masking” is not a standard forensic term used for the internal transport of narcotic substances.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Lines of Langer:

  • The arrangement of the dense network of collagen and elastic fibers in the dermis is referred to as the cleavage direction, while its linear representation on the skin is known as Langer’s lines.

Impact of skin tension:

  • Skin tension and Langer’s lines can change round skin defects into elongated wounds that resemble stab wounds.
  • They can also affect genuine stab wounds, making them appear artificially lengthened.
  • The shape of the wounds also depends on the cleavage lines of Langer.

Assessing wound angles:

  • It may be necessary to bring the wound margins together to determine if a wound angle is sharp or blunt.
  • Holding the edges together aids in a clearer evaluation of the angles.

Variability in injury presentation:

  • Identical weapons can cause different types of injuries based on their location and orientation on the body, influenced by skin elasticity and the alignment of Langer’s lines.
  • A stab wound parallel to the Langer’s lines appears slit-shaped and narrow
  • A stab wound that cuts through the Langer’s lines transversely will gape.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 203.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario points to Harakiri, which is a method of suicide done by the victim using a short sword to inflict a single large stab L-shaped wound in the abdomen leading to a severe loss of blood volume causes the body to enter hypovolemic shock, leading to a sudden drop in intraabdominal pressure and thus causing cardiac collapse and death.

Hara-kiri/Seppukku

  • Hara-kiri refers to an unusual method of suicide where the victim inflicts a single large stab wound on the abdomen.
  • It is associated with Japanese samurai warriors.

Characteristics of the wound

It is a single large stab wound made by the victim by moving the sword across the abdomen (usually left to right) and then turning it up to form an L-shape.

Mechanism of injury
  • The wound is made by a short sword while in a sitting position or
  • By falling onto a ceremonial sword.
  • A well-fixed knife can produce a wound like this, but only with enough momentum to do so.

Cause of death

  • The rapid, severe loss of blood volume causes the body to enter hypovolemic shock, leading to a sudden drop in blood pressure and failure of the circulatory system to deliver enough oxygen to the brain and vital organs. Death typically follows quickly from blood loss.
  • This leads to sudden cardiac collapse and death.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

question:
An old method of suicide conducted by Japanese samurai warriors as a ritual is shown below.

Identify the cause of death in such cases.

correctAnswer: D. The heel of the axe leaves a deeper wound than the toe of the axe
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A chop wound is produced by heavy, sharp weapons like an axe, hatchet, or machete. It shows features of both incised and lacerated wounds due to the combination of sharp and blunt force.

  • Chop wounds often involve bone, causing cuts, chips, or fractures. The wound margins may appear clean superficially but have underlying tissue bridging due to crushing.
  • The heel of the axe (the part closest to the handle) strikes with greater force because it has more control and impact. Thus, the heel produces a deeper wound than the toe (the far end).
  • Dimensions of a chop wound typically correspond to the weapon size. These characteristics help forensic experts determine the weapon type and the force applied.

The wound is a laceration on the surface and does not involve the underlying bone (Option A): Chop wounds frequently involve bone, causing fractures or grooves. They are not simple lacerations.


The dimensions of the wound do not correspond to the weapon size (Option B): Chop wounds usually match the width and shape of the weapon blade. Useful in weapon identification.


The margins of the wound are always irregular (Option C): Margins are often clean and incised, not always irregular. Irregularity appears only when associated with crushing or splitting.



Reference:
  1. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 149
  2. Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 200

question: A 30-year-old woman was attacked with an axe and suffered a chop wound from it. Which of the following is true about a chop wound?

correctAnswer: B. Active defense injuries sustained while attempting to grasp the weapon
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The wound in the given scenario points to an active defense wound where the victim has tried to grasp the weapon to prevent the attack and sustained injuries to the palm and on the fingers which would have been the case with a double-edged weapon.

Defence wounds are caused by the immediate and instinctive reaction of the victim to save himself from an attack and are usually seen on the extremities.

They are divided into two types:

Active defense wounds

Passive defense wounds

Mechanism of injury

The victim tries to grasp the weapon

The victim raises the arms, legs, or hands

Site

  • Depends on the type of weapon.
  • A single-edged weapon causes a single cut on the palm or the bends of fingers or thumb.
  • A double-edged weapon produces cuts on both the palm and fingers.
  • A typical knife defense wound is seen between the base of the thumb and the index finger.
  • Extensor or ulnar surfaces of the forearms, wrists, back of the hands, knuckle. (Option A)
  • Rarely on the shin and feet.
  • Arms and posterior aspect of lower limbs and back.

Type of Injuries

Irregular and ragged cuts due to loosening of skin tension while gripping the knife.

Fractures of the carpal bones, metacarpals, and digits (mostly blunt trauma). (Option D)

[[figure-1]]


Lacerations from a blunt weapon (Option C) are usually split lacerations when a part of the body gets crushed against a hard surface and causes injury. They have sharp edges (incised-looking laceration) unless much skin is involved and are seen mostly over areas with underlying bony prominences like eyebrows, forehead, etc.


Injuries caused by falling onto sharp objects (Option D) can be puncture, penetrating, or perforating wounds, which have clean-cut margins and usually have the dimensions of the weapon causing it.



Reference:
  1. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 156-158
  2. Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Pages 195, 201, 206

question: A victim of an attack displays several injuries on the palms, flexor sides of the fingers, and interdigital spaces and are irregular and ragged cuts. Which of the following best describes the nature of these injuries?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An abrasion is an injury involving the destruction of the full thickness of the epidermis without involving the dermis. Since the dermis contains blood vessels, a pure abrasion does not bleed profusely but may show pinpoint bleeding from the dermal papillae.


Partial thickness of epidermis (Option A): Partial thickness describes a scratch, not an abrasion.


Epidermis with superficial dermis (Option C): If the superficial dermis is involved, it is a graze-laceration.


Epidermis with full dermis (Option D): Full dermis involvement results in a laceration, which heals with a permanent scar; true abrasions heal without scarring.

Reddy KSN. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 35th Edition, Page 162
question: A road traffic accident victim is noted to have the injuries shown in the image given below. These injuries involve loss of skin limited to which layer?

correctAnswer: C. Terminal tailing of the lesion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In a sliding or "graze" abrasion, the friction of the rough surface causes the epidermis to be pushed forward. The injury starts broad and shallow and ends with a "tail" or tapering at the point where the object lost contact with the skin.


Presence of epidermal tags (Option A): Epidermal tags are found at the distal end (the end toward which the force was directed).


Marginal bruising (Option B): Marginal bruising indicates impact but provides no direction..


Crushed hair shafts (Option D): Crushed hair shafts are seen in blunt force trauma (contusions/lacerations) and do not signify the direction.

question: During medicolegal examination, an abrasion shows tapering at one end due to sliding contact. Which feature best determines the direction in which the force was applied?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Graze abrasion (sliding/scrape abrasion) occurs due to horizontal or tangential friction between skin and a hard rough surface.
  • It shows uneven longitudinal parallel lines, which indicate the direction of force applied.
  • The superficial epidermis gets pushed forward and becomes heaped up at the opposite end of the abrasion.
  • Therefore, the direction of epidermal heaping helps determine the direction of force.

Presence of embedded foreign particles (glass, gravel, or dirt) (Option A): Foreign particles may be embedded in graze abrasions, especially in road traffic accidents. They help identify the nature of the causative surface but do not determine the direction of force.

Marginal bruising (Option B): Marginal bruising may occur due to associated tissue trauma but does not provide information regarding the direction of applied force.

Crushed hair shafts (Option D): Crushed hair shafts may be seen in blunt force injuries but do not indicate the direction of force applied.



Reference:

Gautam Biswas, Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 53rd Edition, Page 189-190.

question: During a medicolegal examination, a graze (sliding/scrape) abrasion is observed following a road traffic accident. The abrasion shows parallel longitudinal lines with epidermis heaped up at one end. Which feature helps determine the direction of force applied?

correctAnswer: B. Injuries sustained after death show active bleeding
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Active bleeding requires blood pressure generated by a beating heart. Postmortem wounds are characterised by a lack of bleeding, or at most, a small amount of passive, non-clotting blood seepage due to gravity.


Injuries inflicted during life show an inflammatory response (Option A): Antemortem injuries trigger the body's defensive inflammatory cascade.


Postmortem injuries lack tissue reaction (Option C): Postmortem injuries occur in dead tissue where cellular respiration and circulation have ceased, hence no tissue reaction.


Antemortem injuries exhibit tissue response (Option D): Antemortem injuries show signs like retraction of wound edges and clotting.



Reference:

Pillay VV. Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 19th Edition, Page 184

question: Which of the following statements regarding wounds and vital reactions is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Wound description: When describing a stab wound, it’s important to note the length, width, direction, and appearance of the wound's margins and angles.

Margins
  • The edges of the wound are clean-cut (statement 3) and typically show no abrasion or bruisin
  • In cases of full blade penetration, a patterned abrasion or bruising may occur due to the hilt guard striking the skin
  • The margins are regular, sharp, and well-defined; however, wounds caused by pointed or conical instruments may have lacerated edges
Length
  • The length of the wound is usually slightly less than the width (statement 4) of the weapon because of skin stretching
Breadth
  • The breadth maybe equal to, less than/greater than the thickness of the blade (statement 1) due to gaping; proper approximation of the edges is necessary for accurate measurement
Depth
  • Depth is the greatest dimension of a stab wound (statement 2) and corresponds to the length of the weapon entering the body
  • If the entire length of the weapon penetrates without producing an exit wound, this depth is critical
Safety note:
  • It is unsafe to determine the depth of a stab wound by probing in the emergency room, as this can disturb any loose clot and lead to severe hemorrhage
  • Probing may also create a false track by passing between fascial planes or within muscles
  • Depth assessment should be conducted in the operating theater during wound repair



Reference:

Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 201
question:
A forensic surgeon is examining a stab wound on a victim. Which of the following statement/s is/are true about the dimensions of the wound?

  1. Breadth of the wound is equal to the thickness of the weapon
  2. Depth is the greatest dimension of a stab wound
  3. The edges of the wound are clean-cut
  4. The length of the wound is usually slightly more than the width

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Histological/Microscopic examination is the gold standard. It identifies specific cellular timelines:

  • Neutrophils (6-12 hrs),
  • Macrophages (24-48 hrs), and
  • The appearance of Hemosiderin (approx. 72 hrs).


Gross colour changes (Option A): Gross color changes are unreliable because they depend on the depth of the bruise, the individual's skin color, and the lighting during examination.


Detection of green pigmentation (Option B): Green pigmentation (biliverdin) occurs between 4-7 days, not very specific.


Chemical staining alone (Option D): Chemical staining (Prussian Blue) is a part of histology, but does not give as complete a picture as total microscopic tissue assessment.

question: A forensic expert is asked to estimate the age of a contusion in a suspected assault victim. Which method provides the most reliable estimation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image denotes postmortem lividity/ livor mortis.

Incising the discoloured area refers to the incision test. In a bruise, the blood has leaked into the tissues (extravasated) and cannot be washed away. In postmortem lividity, the blood is still inside the vessels; when incised, it can be easily washed off.


Gettler’s test (Option A): The Gettler Test or Chloride Test is a forensic method used to help determine if death was caused by drowning and differentiate between freshwater and saltwater drowning by measuring chloride levels in blood.


Benzidine test (Option C): The Benzidine test only confirms the presence of blood, not its origin. It reacts with heme iron in hemoglobin, turning from clear to deep blue in the presence of blood, thereby aiding in preliminary crime scene analysis.


Precipitin reaction (Option D): The precipitin reaction is used to identify the species of origin for biological stains like blood, semen, or saliva, by mixing an extract of the stain with specific antisera (e.g., rabbit anti-human serum) to form a visible, insoluble antigen-antibody complex (precipitate), proving if the sample is human or animal



Reference:

Gautam Biswas. Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 5th Edition, Page 156
question: At autopsy, discoloration is noted over dependent areas of the body. Which procedure helps confirm whether the finding represents true bruising?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A double-edged weapon (like a dagger) produces a symmetrical, spindle-shaped or "wedge-like" wound because both ends of the blade are sharp, resulting in both angles of the wound being acute.


Single-edged blade (Option A): A single-edged blade produces a "V-shaped" wound where one end is sharp, and the other is squared off (blunt).


Serrated knife (Option B): Serrated knives produce jagged/irregular margins.


Blunt metallic rod (Option D): Blunt rods produce circular or irregular puncture-lacerations.



Reference:

Reddy KSN. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 35th Edition, Page 187
question: A penetrating injury with symmetrical margins and a wedge-like appearance is observed during examination. Which weapon is most consistent with this injury?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A single-edged weapon produces a wedge-shaped or triangular stab wound in which one angle is sharp while the opposite angle is blunt, rounded, or squared off.

  • The blunt end may show small skin splits known as “fish-tailing.”
  • These features are characteristic of stab wounds caused by single-edged knives.

Double-edged blade (Option B): Produces an elliptical or slit-like wound with both angles sharp and symmetrical.

Spear (Option C): A round or pointed spear typically produces circular puncture wounds.

Screwdriver (Option D): Produces slit-like stab wounds with squared ends and abraded margins rather than wedge-shaped injuries.



Reference:

Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology by Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Pages 202, 205

An incised wound is caused by a sharp edge that cleanly divides all tissues, including "nicking" or cutting the bone in a linear fashion.


Hair shaft bridging and tissue bridges (Option B & C): These are pathognomonic for lacerations (blunt force), as these structures are more resistant to tearing than skin.


Surrounding contusions at the wound margins (Option D): They are typical of the impact of a laceration.

question: While examining a cut injury produced over a bony surface, which of the following findings would favour an incised wound rather than a split laceration?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Swallow tailing occurs when a blunt object (like a car bumper) strikes the skin at an angle. The force "undermines" the skin and tears it in two directions at the end, resembling the tail of a swallow.


Sparrow’s foot (Option A): It is a characteristic, small, V-shaped laceration on the face or limbs caused by shattering tempered glass, typically from a car windshield during a road accident, resembling bird tracks.


Wedging (Option B): Wedging is seen in single-edged stab wounds.


Fish tailing (Option C): Fish tailing refers to a characteristic tear or blunt/triangular shape at one end of a stab wound, indicating a single-edged knife made it.

question: A blunt force injury produces a laceration with characteristic radiating skin tears at both ends. What is this appearance called?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Trial cuts (Hesitation marks) are superficial, parallel incisions made by a person before they summon the courage to make a deep, fatal cut. They are highly suggestive of suicide.


Defence injuries (Option A): Defence wounds are found mostly on the palms or outer forearm and are usually deep and irregular.


Self-mutilation (Option B): Self-mutilation is the deliberate, direct destruction or alteration of body tissue without conscious suicidal intent.


Accidental sharp injury (Option D): Accidental injuries lack this organised, parallel pattern.

question: During autopsy, several superficial, parallel, linear cuts are observed along the ulnar aspect of the forearm. These findings are most suggestive of which manner of injury?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The emigration of Polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocytes from the capillaries into the wound site is a vital reaction that typically begins within 4 to 8 hours and becomes prominent by 12 hours.


Within 2 hours (Option A), we only see biochemical changes (histamine/serotonin).


Between 12-24 hours (Option C) is when infiltration is peaking, but it starts much earlier.


After 72 hours (Option D), the predominant cells are macrophages and fibroblasts.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Imprint abrasions occur when a patterned object, like a vehicle tyre or a textured surface, presses against the skin, leaving a distinct impression of the object. In this case, the patterned nature of the injury suggests an imprint abrasion.

Abrasion:

Abrasion is a superficial injury caused by the removal or damage of the skin's outer layer (epidermis) due to friction or pressure. It is classified into four main types:

[[figure-1]]

Scratch Abrasion (Linear Abrasion) (Option A)

Grazed Abrasion (Sliding Abrasion) (Option B)
  • Mechanism: Caused by tangential (side-to-side) force, producing a long and narrow abrasion.
  • Features: Linear in nature, with length being more significant than width.
  • Examples: Fingernail abrasion, thorn abrasion, and pin abrasion.

[[figure-2]]
  • Mechanism: Occurs when skin slides over a rough surface, resulting in superficial scrapes.
  • Also Known As: Grinding abrasion, gravel rash, brush-burn.
  • Features: Seen in road traffic accidents or falls, especially on exposed areas like knees or elbows.

[[figure-3]]

Imprint Abrasion (Patterned Abrasion) (Option C)

Pressure Abrasion (Crushing Abrasion) (Option D)
  • Mechanism: Results from compressive force applied perpendicular to the skin, leaving a distinct pattern of the object.
  • Also Known As Impact abrasion, contact abrasion, patterned abrasion.
  • Examples: Tyre marks, bite marks.

[[figure-4]]
  • Mechanism: Caused by a continuous vertical force applied to the skin, crushing the epidermis.
  • Features: Deeper skin injuries are often seen with prolonged pressure, potentially leading to necrosis.
  • Examples: Ligature marks in hanging or strangulation

[[figure-5]]



Reference:

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 134-136.

[[figure-1]]

Mechanism: Caused by a continuous vertical force (Option D) applied to the skin, crushing the epidermis (Option C).

Features: Deeper skin injuries (Option A) are often seen with prolonged pressure, potentially leading to necrosis.

Examples: Ligature marks in hanging or strangulation.

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 134-136.

question: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department following minor trauma from bumping into a table corner. Physical examination reveals a bluish discoloration on the thigh. Based on its appearance, what is the most likely age of the bruise?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical scenario shows patterned contusions that appear as two parallel, linear hemorrhages with normal skin in between known as tram track or railway line-type contusions.


Contusions/bruises can be classified into two types based on the way they appear:

Ectopic/percolated/migratory bruise

Patterned bruise
  • In deep bruises, blood tracks along the fascial planes and may cause the bruise at a different site.
  • This is also called percolated or migratory contusion.
  • Examples:
    • Spectacle hematoma (Option B) around the eyes after a blunt trauma to the forehead
    • Bruise behind the ear due to basal skull fracture known as Battle sign (Option A)
    • Bruise in thigh due to fractured pelvis
    • Bruise around knee due to a kick on calf
    • Grey Turner’s sign: Ecchymosis seen over the flank or side of the abdomen due to extensive retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
      Takes 24-48 hours to develop
    • Cullen’s sign: Bluish-black discoloration of the periumbilical skin due to extensive retroperitoneal or intraabdominal bleeding.
      Causes can be ruptured ectopic pregnancy or acute pancreatitis
  • The shape and size of the bruise resemble a part of the object that caused it.
  • Shapes of bruises by different weapons:
    • A solid body like a hammer or fist causes round bruises
    • A doughnut bruise due to objects like a cricket ball
    • A rod, stick, or whip leads to two parallel, linear hemorrhages with normal skin in between known as railway line or tram line bruises
    • Blows from a whip are elongated and partially encircle a limb or the body
    • Tire patterns from an automobile accident (Option D)

question:
A 30-year-old man presents with multiple bruises on his body following a fight. Upon examination, the physician notes a specific pattern of bruising on his back as shown:

What is this type of bruise called?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The sign here is the Grey Turner’s sign which is the ecchymosis seen over the flank or side of the abdomen due to extensive retroperitoneal hemorrhage which is a type of migratory or ectopic bruise.

Gravity shifting of blood (ectopic/migratory bruise):

  • Bruises may appear at sites distant from the actual injury (e.g., black eyes).
  • The blood tracks along fascial planes or between muscle layers, following the path of least resistance, leading to bruising in superficial tissue areas.
  • Therefore, the location of a bruise does not always reflect the site of injury.

Grey Turner’s sign:

  • Ecchymosis observed over the flank or side of the abdomen which is indicative of extensive retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
  • This sign typically develops within 24–48 hours.

Cullen’s Sign: (Option C)

  • Bluish-black discoloration around the periumbilical area resulting from extensive retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
  • Common causes include ruptured ectopic pregnancy or acute pancreatitis.
  • Other examples:
    • Spectacle hematoma (Option A) around the eyes after a blunt trauma to the forehead
    • Bruise behind the ear due to basal skull fracture known as Battle sign (Option D)
    • Bruise in thigh due to fractured pelvis
    • Bruise around the knee due to a kick on the calf



Reference:
  1. Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 192
  2. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 139
question: Given below is the picture of a patient with history of fall from a bike the day before. What is the name of this finding?

correctAnswer: B. Artificial bruising to falsely accuse someone
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario here shows a bruise that is dark brown and irregularly shaped with well-defined margins and redness and inflammation of the surrounding tissues that point to artificial bruises.

Contusions can be divided as follows:

Artificial bruising

True bruising (Option A)
  • These are bruises created to make a false charge of assault.
  • They are usually present on accessible parts of the body.
  • They appear dark brown and irregular in shape.
  • Redness and inflammation are seen in the surrounding tissues.
  • Produced by the juice of a marking nut rubbed on the body.
  • Well-defined margins with small vesicles.
  • Itching is present.
  • Other substances used:
    • Plumbago
    • Madar/calotropis
    • Semicardium

[[figure-1]]
  • The cause of true bruising is trauma.
  • They can be located anywhere in the body.
  • They undergo typical color changes.
  • Redness and inflammation are seen on the site.
  • They are usually round with well-defined, diffuse, and irregular margins with no vesicles.
  • They have extravasated blood as content and are not associated with itching.

[[figure-2]]

Postmortem bruising from blood settling (Option C):

  • An injury produced before death may lead to a bruise later due to further escape of blood.
  • A deep bruise may appear several hours or 1-2 days later, and deeper extravasation of blood may not appear at all.
  • Caused by percolation and rapid hemolysis of stagnant blood, leading to the pigment being diffused locally.
  • This produces a stain on the surface called a come-out bruise.
  • Some bruises are difficult to detect, and hence, the examination of the whole body under UV light helps locate them.

Bruising due to pre-existing medical conditions (Option D) like arteriosclerosis, purpura, leukemia, hemophilia, scurvy, etc., causes easy bruising but appears different from an artificial bruise, and a clear history of these diseases is present.



Reference:

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 139, 142

question:
A medicolegal case of assault is being examined at the emergency with the following contusions.

What is the most likely explanation for the appearance of these bruises?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Laceration results from blunt force trauma rather than sharp force. It leads to irregular, jagged wounds caused by tearing of the tissue.

Classification of Mechanical Injuries

Blunt Force Injuries

Sharp Force Injuries
  • Abrasion: Superficial damage to the skin (scraping, rubbing off the outer layer).
  • Contusion: Bruise caused by blood vessels rupturing under the skin due to impact.
  • Laceration: Irregular tear in the skin or tissue caused by crushing or blunt trauma.
  • Fractures/Dislocations: Breaks or misalignment of bones due to strong blunt impact.
  • Incision: A clean-cut wound where the length is greater than the depth.
  • Stab Wound: A deep wound where the depth is greater than the length.
  • Chop Wound: A deep wound often associated with underlying fractures caused by heavy-bladed tools like an axe.



Reference:

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 133, 134.

Parikhs Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 8th Edition, Page 222.
question: Which of the following is not a cause of injury due to sharp force?

correctAnswer: B. Laceration caused by blunt force trauma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The irregular edges, bruising, and embedded dirt indicate a laceration resulting from blunt force. Such wounds often show uneven tearing and damage to underlying structures like nerves and blood vessels, consistent with the autopsy findings.

Laceration

  • Laceration is the tearing or splitting of the skin, mucous membranes, muscles, or internal organs due to a shearing or crushing force from a blunt impact over a broad area.
  • When blunt force causes severe bruising and damage to deeper tissues, it is referred to as a crush injury.

Characteristics

[[figure-1]]

  • Irregular Margins: Ragged, uneven edges with pointed or blunt ends, often showing small tears.
  • Swallow Tails: Tearing at the ends of lacerations, diverging.
  • Bruising: Seen around the wound, more pronounced in areas impacted at an angle or with downward force.
  • Tissue Bridges: Deeper tissues are unevenly torn, leaving nerve, vessel, and connective tissue bridges.
  • Hair Damage: Crushed hair bulbs; hair and skin tags may be embedded in the wound.
  • Hemorrhage: Less severe bleeding as arteries are crushed and torn irregularly, retracting and allowing blood to clot.
  • Soiling: Debris like mud, wood splinters, sand, glass, or hair can become embedded, carrying medico-legal significance.
  • Wound Gaping: Impact from an angle causes tearing on the opposite side and abrasion on the impact side, leading to gaping.


Incised wounds (Option A) have clean, smooth edges and do not show the uneven tearing or bruising present in this case.


Abrasions (Option C) involve superficial skin damage and typically lack deep tissue involvement and significant bruising.


Puncture wounds (Option D) are small and deep, usually causing localized damage without the extensive tearing or irregular margins seen here.



Reference:
  1. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 144, 145
  2. Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 197

question: During an autopsy, the forensic pathologist observes an injury on the thigh, which shows irregular edges, bruising, and embedded dirt. On further examination, the deeper tissues show uneven tearing, with visible nerve and blood vessel damage. What type of injury is most consistent with these findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Split lacerations are commonly seen in areas where the skin is close to bone, such as the scalp, with minimal underlying soft tissue. Although the edges may appear sharp, the presence of tissue bridges confirms the diagnosis of a laceration rather than an incised wound.


Types of Laceration

  • Split laceration
  • Avulsion laceration
  • Stretch laceration
  • Tear laceration
  • Cut laceration

Types of Laceration

[[figure-1]]

Split Laceration (Option B)
  • These occur when skin is crushed between two objects, such as the scalp being compressed between the skull and a hard surface like the ground or a blunt object.
  • Seen on areas where the skin is close to bone, with minimal underlying tissue
  • E.g., scalp, eyebrows, cheekbones, jaw, iliac crest, perineum, shin.
  • Lacerations without excessive skin crushing can have sharp edges, resembling incised wounds.
  • Also known as incised looking laceration.
  • These are not undermined and show tissue bridges.

[[figure-2]]

Avulsion (Shearing Laceration) (Option C)
  • Caused by a shearing force at an acute angle, detaching skin or organs from their attachments.
  • The shearing and grinding force from a heavy object, like a lorry wheel passing over a limb, can cause the skin to separate from the underlying tissues, a condition known as avulsion or "flaying."
  • This often results in crushed muscles and fractured bones. The detached skin may have extensive abrasions due to the tyre’s friction, but one portion is still in continuity with adjacent skin.
  • Lacerations from shearing forces can leave the skin intact while separating the underlying soft tissue from the fascia, resulting in a blood-filled pocket. This type of injury is often observed on the back of the thighs in pedestrians hit by motor vehicles.


Incised wounds (Option A) have clean, sharp edges from a cutting instrument. The presence of tissue bridges in this case indicates it is a split laceration rather than a clean cut.


Chop wounds (Option D) involve significant tissue damage from extreme pressure. The sharp-edged, localized laceration with minimal underlying tissue damage does not fit the profile of a chop wound.



Reference:

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 143, 144
question: A 50-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after hitting her head on a metal beam. On examination, the wound has sharp edges but lacks undermining, and tissue bridges are visible. There is no significant underlying soft tissue present between the skin and the skull. What is the most likely type of injury?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Stretch laceration occurs from overstretching of skin, commonly seen in motor vehicle accidents. The presence of a skin flap, irregular tissue tearing, and embedded foreign materials are typical characteristics. Additionally, the skin flap's orientation helps infer the direction of the vehicle's movement, which is consistent with stretch lacerations.

Types of Laceration

[[figure-1]]

Stretch laceration (Option C)

  • Caused by overstretching of fixed skin, leading to localized pressure and tearing, which creates a skin flap
  • Commonly seen in motor vehicle accidents, with the skin flap potentially indicating the vehicle's direction.
  • Can occur from kicking or bone deformity after a fracture, leading to compound injuries.
  • Results in irregular skin and tissue tearing, with a risk of foreign materials entering the wound.

Tear lacerations (Option D)

Cut Lacerations (Option B)
  • Result from impact with irregular or semi-sharp objects (e.g., car door handles, broken glass).
  • Characterized by a deeper starting point that tapers off towards the end, representing another form of overstretching.
  • Produced by heavy, sharp-edged instruments (e.g., axes, hatchets).
  • Typically, they have abraded margins with bruising, although the term "cut laceration" is often considered less precise.


Chop/ Slash wound (Option A)

[[figure-2]]

  • Deep, gaping wounds caused by a blow from a sharp-cutting edge of a heavy weapon (e.g., hatchet, axe, sword, chopper).
  • Wound size corresponds to the cross-section of the blade.
  • Undermining occurs in the direction of chop.
  • The heel (lower end) of the axe typically strikes first, leading to deeper wounds than the toe (upper end).
  • The deeper end indicates the assailant's position.
  • Clean slicing through bone at impact; rebound can create irregular fragments; may lead to complete or incomplete amputations.
  • Mostly homicidal injuries to exposed body parts (head, face, neck, extremities)


Reference:

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 144, 149
question: A 32-year-old male was involved in a high-speed motor vehicle accident. Upon examination, the direction of the vehicle's movement can be inferred from the orientation of the skin flap, as shown in the image below. What is the most likely type of injury in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image shows an Incised wound with clean and well-defined edges.


Incised wounds

  • An incised wound is a clean cut through the skin and subcutaneous tissues, typically longer than it is deep, caused by a sharp-edged instrument like a knife or razor.
  • It results from pressure and friction against the tissue.

[[figure-1]]

Wound Structure:

  • Margins: Clean, well-defined edges (Option D), often everted; may appear inverted with adhered muscle fibers. No contusions or abrasions (Option B), but may show wrinkling with multiple incisions. No bridging tissue.
  • Width: Greater than the weapon's cutting edge due to tissue retraction.
  • Length: Exceeds width and depth, with no relation to the weapon's edge.
  • Shape: Usually spindle-shaped, with more gaping in the center; gaping is influenced by the direction of cuts across skin fibers.
  • Hemorrhage: Significant bleeding occurs from cleanly cut vessels. (Option C)

Tailing

Bevelling
  • Deeper at the beginning due to greater knife pressure (the "head" of the wound). (Option A)
  • Becomes shallower toward the exit.
  • Indicating the cutting direction.
  • A wound created by an obliquely entering blade features a beveled margin on one side, and an undermined area on the other side.
  • Characteristic of sharp weapons
  • Associated with homicidal injuries.
  • Suggest the positions of the assailant and victim.



Reference:

The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K. S. Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 146, 147.

correctAnswer: A. The individual experienced a moment of hesitation before the fatal injury.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of small, superficial cuts around a deeper wound suggests a possible moment of doubt or fear before inflicting the fatal injury. These small cuts can be indicative of hesitation, often observed in scenarios of self-infliction or in cases where the victim may have struggled before the lethal wound.

Hesitation cuts:

[[figure-1]]

  • Hesitation cuts (also known as tentative cuts or trial wounds) are multiple, small, superficial cuts that typically involve only the skin.
  • These cuts are often found at the beginning of a deeper incised wound.
  • Psychological Aspect: They suggest that the individual may have hesitated while gathering the courage to make a decisive cut.
  • Forensic Observation: In cases of homicidal sharp force injuries, multiple superficial, roughly parallel incised wounds may appear on the neck, often adjacent to a single deep, lethal incised wound, particularly in instances where torture is involved.

Hesitation cuts are associated with sharp objects, not blunt ones. The nature of the wounds indicates a sharp instrument was likely used. (Option B)

The close, parallel cuts suggest the attack occurred at close range, not from a distance. (Option C)

While hesitation marks can appear in self-inflicted wounds, this option is too specific without confirming intent. The wounds could also result from an attack by another individual. (Option D)



Reference:

Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Page 199.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The temporal bone is the most commonly fractured in basilar skull fractures. These fractures can lead to serious complications, including damage to cranial nerves VII (facial nerve) and VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) and the carotid artery, as well as potential cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks.

Temporal bone fracture

Longitudinal Temporal Bone Fracture

Transverse Temporal Bone Fracture
  • The most common type (70-90% of temporal bone fractures).
  • Runs parallel to the long axis of the petrous temporal bone.
  • Otic Capsule is spared.
  • Conductive hearing loss due to ossicle involvement and tympanic membrane involvement.
  • Facial nerve involvement occurs in about 25% of cases.
  • Less common (10-30% of temporal bone fractures).
  • Extends perpendicular to the petrous temporal bone's long axis.
  • Otic Capsule is involved, leading to sensorineural hearing loss.
  • Ossicles and tympanic membranes are generally unaffected.
  • Higher incidence of facial nerve involvement.


Occipital bone (Option B), Sphenoid bone (Option C), Frontal bone (Option D): While the occipital, sphenoid, and frontal bones can be involved in basilar skull fractures, they are not as commonly fractured as the temporal bone. Their occurrences are significantly less frequent compared to fractures of the temporal bone.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Fissured Fracture (Linear Fracture)

Diastatic Fracture (Sutural Fracture)

  • The most common skull fracture accounts for about 70% of cases.
  • Linear cracks may involve the vertex or skull base. It can affect the full thickness of the bone or just the inner/outer layers.
  • The fracture line is irregular and fine, sometimes hard to detect on X-rays. It runs parallel to the compressive force.
  • No depression of bone fragments.
  • Involves the separation of cranial sutures.
  • More common in children.
  • Often occurs with other skull fractures, especially fissured fractures.
  • Commonly seen at the sagittal suture.

Causes:

  • Impact against broad surfaces (e.g., falls or road traffic accidents). (Option A ruled out)
  • Falls on feet or buttocks, transmitting force upwards. (Option D ruled out)

Causes:

  • Blunt trauma to the head.
  • Increased intracranial pressure leads to suture separation. (Option B)

Narrow fissure skull fracture

[[figure-2]]

A teenager experiencing a sports-related injury (Option C): Sports-related injuries typically do not involve sutural separation, which is specific to diastatic fractures.

question: In which of the following scenarios is a diastatic skull fracture most likely to occur?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Depressed Fracture

Comminuted Fracture

Gutter Fracture
  • Occurs when a fragment of the skull is pushed inward towards the brain.
  • Caused by blows from heavy objects with a small surface (e.g., hammers, bricks). (Option A ruled out)
  • The shape of the depressed area may resemble the object that caused the injury.

Variants:

  • Elevated Fracture: One end of the fractured fragment is raised above the skull, while the other is pushed inward. Caused by sharp objects like an axe. (Option D ruled out)
  • Pond Fracture: Seen in infants, this smooth depression occurs without a fracture line, resembling a dent in a ping-pong ball. Caused by obstetrics forceps blade.
  • Involves multiple intersecting fracture lines, breaking the bone into several fragments.
  • Caused by high-impact trauma (e.g., vehicular accidents, crushing injuries). (Option C ruled out)
  • It may occur alongside other fractures (e.g., fissured or depressed fractures).
  • Spider web-like patterns on an X-ray are characteristic of comminuted fractures.
  • In severe cases, bone fragments may penetrate the brain or become displaced.
  • A groove or channel is formed in the skull bone, often due to an oblique bullet wound. (Option B)
  • Frequently associated with comminuted and depressed fractures of the inner skull table.
  • Bone fragments can cause injury to the meninges or brain.

question: A “motorcyclist fracture," typically results from what type of impact?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Blowout fracture is a fracture of the bony orbit (eye socket) resulting from blunt trauma to the eye. It causes fractures to the medial wall and floor of the orbit. The teardrop sign is a significant radiographic finding in blowout fractures, indicating the herniation of orbital soft tissues, such as fat and muscles, into the maxillary sinus. This often leads to pain, restricted eye movements and diplopia.

[[figure-1]]

Blowout fracture of the right orbit showing the teardrop sign


Spider web-like pattern on X-ray (Option A): The spider web-like pattern on an X-ray is characteristic of comminuted fractures, which involve multiple fracture lines creating a fragmented appearance.


Ping-pong ball dent appearance (Option B): The ping-pong ball dent appearance is associated with pond fractures, which occur in infants and young children. This type of fracture is characterised by a smooth, concave indentation in the skull without a distinct fracture line.


Circular crack around the skull base (Option D): A circular crack around the skull base is indicative of a ring fracture, which encircles the foramen magnum and is associated with severe trauma.

correctAnswer: C. Contrecoup injuries primarily affect the areas directly beneath the point of impact
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Coup injuries primarily affect the areas directly beneath the point of impact, while contrecoup injuries affect the side opposite the impact.

Coup vs. Contrecoup Injuries

Features

Coup

Contrecoup

Definition

Brain injury directly beneath the point of impact.

Brain injury on the side opposite the impact.

Mechanism

Caused by direct impact force.

Occurs when a moving head is suddenly decelerated by hitting a firm surface eg. striking the head on the ground after a fall during RTAs. (Option B ruled out)

Occurrence

More common when a moving object strikes the head.

Common in falls or blows to a stationary head.

Common scenarios

Common in moving head striking an object, e.g., hitting a car dashboard in an accident.

Seen in falls, where the head hits the ground or an unyielding surface, causing injury on the opposite side of the impact.

Organs involved

It can be seen in the brain, heart, spleen and lungs. (More commonly in the brain)

Theories of Contrecoup Injuries:

  • Shear Strain Theory (Holbourn): Brain particles are pulled apart due to rotational forces. (Option D ruled out)
  • Vacuum Theory: A vacuum or cavity forms in the cranial cavity, exerting suction on the brain opposite the point of impact, causing damage.
  • Deceleration Theory: Sudden arrest of the head causes the brain to strike the skull at the opposite pole of impact.

Common scenarios:

  • Occipital impact: Produces frontal contrecoup injury due to brain displacement against the frontal lobes. (Option A ruled out)
  • Temporal or parietal impact: Results in contralateral contrecoup injury on the opposite side of the brain.
  • Top of the head impact: Can cause ventral surface contusion of the cerebral hemisphere.
  • Frontal region impact: May not produce occipital contrecoup injury due to the smooth internal surface of the posterior cranial fossa



Reference:
  1. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 192, 193
  2. www.researchgate.net/publication/276136525_Significance_of_Contre-Coup_Injury_in_Trauma_to_Brain_for_Concluding_Manner_of_Death_A_Case_Report

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The subarachnoid space is situated between the arachnoid mater and pia mater and contains major arteries, including those of the circle of Willis.

  • This space is usually filled with clear, colourless cerebrospinal fluid.
  • Head trauma or rupture of an intracranial aneurysm causes a subarachnoid haemorrhage (bleeding in the subarachnoid space).
  • The most common specific locations of intracranial aneurysms are at the middle cerebral artery bifurcation and along the anterior communicating artery.

[[figure-1]]

Meningeal layers

Intracranial haemorrhages

  • The first layer is the skull vault (cranium), followed by the dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater, and brain tissue (cerebrum).
  • The space between the skull and dura contains the middle meningeal artery.
  • The middle meningeal artery is most prominent at the pterion, the point where the frontal, parietal, sphenoid, and temporal bones meet.

Space

Location

Blood vessel involved

Epidural Space

Between the skull vault and dura mater. The collection of blood here leads to epidural hematoma.

Middle meningeal artery

(Option D ruled out)

Subdural Space

Between the arachnoid and dura mater. The collection of blood here leads to subdural hematoma. (Option B ruled out)

Bridging veins (which drain into the dural venous sinus)

(Option A ruled out)

Subarachnoid Space

Between the arachnoid and pia mater

Arteries of the circle of Willis (Middle cerebral artery, Anterior communicating artery -most commonly) (Option C)

question: In the context of intracranial haemorrhages, which of the following statements accurately describes the relationship between the layers of the cranial anatomy and the associated blood vessels?

correctAnswer: B. Rupture of the middle meningeal artery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The CT scan of the patient showing a biconvex accumulation of blood between the skull and dura mater after a fall confirms the diagnosis of EDH. EDH is primarily caused by trauma leading to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery.


Extradural Hemorrhage (Epidural Hemorrhage)

Anatomy: The dura mater is a strong, grey-bluish connective tissue membrane. Its outer layer adheres to the skull, and the inner layer merges with the arachnoid.

Causes:

  • Primarily caused by trauma, resulting in the skull moving relative to the dura and creating an extradural space.
  • Injury Sites: Commonly due to fractures of the squamous temporal bone, leading to injury of the middle meningeal artery (posterior branch).

Clinical Features:

  • Initial Symptoms: History of head injury; may include temporary unconsciousness.
  • Lucid Interval: A period (30-40% of cases) after initial unconsciousness, where the patient regains awareness, lasting 2-4 hours to a week before neurological symptoms decline.
  • Progression: Increased intracranial pressure can lead to confusion, lethargy, coma, and neurological signs such as contralateral weakness, dilated pupils (initially on the side of haemorrhage), and possible decerebrate rigidity.
  • Fatality: Typically associated with a minimum haemorrhage volume of 100 ml, often due to respiratory failure from brainstem compression.

Imaging: Brain CT scans show a biconvex or lens-shaped mass typical of extradural haemorrhage.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment:

  • Craniotomy: Recommended for acute symptomatic extradural hematomas to facilitate complete hematoma evacuation
  • Trephination (Burr Hole Evacuation): Employed when advanced surgical expertise is unavailable, serving as a crucial intervention to reduce mortality
  • Indications include:
    • Hematoma volume > 30 mL on CT scan
    • Hematoma thickness > 15 mm on CT scan
    • Midline shift > 5 mm on CT imaging
    • Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤ 8 with evidence of EDH on imaging
    • Progressive neurological deterioration, such as worsening consciousness or focal neurological deficits
    • Presence of pupillary abnormalities, especially ipsilateral dilated or non-reactive pupil suggesting uncal herniation
    • Signs of raised intracranial pressure, e.g., persistent vomiting, severe headache, bradycardia, hypertension (Cushing reflex)
    • Temporal or posterior fossa EDH, even if small, due to risk of rapid brainstem compression
    • Associated focal neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis)
    • Failure of conservative management or increase in hematoma size on repeat CT scan


Rupture of bridging veins (Option A): This type of injury is associated with subdural haemorrhage, not extradural haemorrhage, and would not produce a biconvex mass on CT.

[[figure-2]]


Venous thrombosis (Option C): While it can lead to increased intracranial pressure, it does not typically result in a localized biconvex mass, as seen in extradural haemorrhage.


Subarachnoid haemorrhage (Option D): This condition presents with diffuse blood in the subarachnoid space rather than a well-defined mass



Reference:
  1. The Essentials of Forensic Medicine, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 196, 197

  3. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23896724/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The gradual onset of symptoms and isodense appearance on CT are characteristic of subacute subdural haemorrhage, typically occurring days to weeks after injury.


Subdural Haemorrhage

  • Anatomy:
    • Subdural space is narrow, between the dura mater and arachnoid.
    • Cerebral (bridging) veins cross this space to reach venous sinuses.

Subacute SDH

Chronic SDH
  • Rapid onset after trauma
  • Rupture of large bridging veins or cortical arteries.
  • The most common symptoms are mental confusion, drowsiness, dilation of the pupil (ipsilateral) and contralateral involvement of hemiparesis.
  • Death may occur if the haemorrhage volume is about 100 to 150 ml.
  • Hyperdense on CT. (Option A ruled out)

[[figure-1]]
  • Symptoms develop over days to weeks after injury.
  • Usually from smaller bridging veins.
  • Isodense on CT

[[figure-2]]
  • Develops weeks or months later
  • Often in the elderly;
  • Slow bleeding leads to gradual symptoms.
  • Symptoms arise weeks/months later;
  • May lead to Subdural Hygroma:-Tear in the arachnoid allows CSF to collect in the subdural space, causing cerebral compression.

[[figure-3]]

    • More extensive than epidural haemorrhage (EDH), covering a larger area.
