question: A forensic pathologist is conducting an autopsy on a 38-year-old male who died after an accidental exposure to hydrofluoric acid (HF) at an industrial plant. Which of the following postmortem findings is most characteristic of HF poisoning?

explanationHtml:
Carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning presents with Gray/brown corrosions on mouth, esophageal burns, a strong antiseptic odor, CNS depression, hypotension and renal failure due to its toxic effects on the central nervous system, cardiovascular system and kidneys.


Phenol Poisoning (Carbolism)

Physical Properties

Colorless, crystalline, turns pink on air exposure; slightly acidic, forms phenolate ion (C6H5O{).

Uses

Antiseptic/disinfectant; Lysol (50% cresol), Dettol (chlorinated phenol with turpineol).

Fatal Dose

1-2 g phenol or 25-50 ml of household phenol.

Fatal Period

3-4 hours.

Tissue Discoloration

Can lead to ochronosis (bluish-black discoloration in tissues like ears and sclera).

Signs and symptoms
  • Local Effects: Tingling → numbness → coagulation necrosis → painless white eschar, which turns brown and sloughs off
  • Gastrointestinal: Initial burning/tingling, later anesthesia; diarrhea and abdominal pain, and vomiting
  • Respiratory: Phenol odor on breath, laryngeal/pulmonary edema, stertorous breathing, cyanosis
  • Metabolized by kidneys into hydroquinone/pyrocatechol; causes carboluria (dark green urine)
  • Cardiovascular (CVS): Rapid, feeble, irregular pulse; cold, clammy skin; collapse, unconsciousness, coma
  • Muscular: Muscle spasms, convulsions
  • CNS: Headache, giddiness, tinnitus, contracted pupils
  • Renal: Dark smoky green color of urine

Postmortem Findings
  • External: Gray/brown corrosion on mouth, body, hands; phenolic odor, delayed putrefaction due to antiseptic properties of phenol
  • Internal: Leather bottle stomach appearance due to protein coagulation, corroded GIT mucosa, pulmonary edema, hemorrhagic nephritis

Medico-legal Aspects

Used in suicides, accidental poisoning, rare for homicides (strong odor/taste), abortifacient.
Management
  • Decontamination: Gastric lavage can be done
  • Adsorbents: Activated charcoal
  • Neutralization: Vegetable oils or glycerin may reduce phenol absorption
  • Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen, correction of hypotension
  • Renal protection: Maintain urine output
  • Symptomatic treatment: Manage seizures, shock, and respiratory distress



Reference:
  1. Goutam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd Edition, Page 486, 487
  2. Parikh's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 8th Edition, Page 557

On examination, his angle of mouth is stained gray, and he has burns on his esophagus. The patient had a history of greenish discoloration of urine. What is the most likely cause of these findings?

explanationHtml:
• Oxalic acid causes hypocalcemia, renal stones, and renal damage, resulting in swollen, congested kidneys with tubular necrosis, along with gelatinous brown content in the stomach.

Feature

HNO₃ (Nitric Acid)

Oxalic Acid

Physical Properties

Colorless, pungent, choking, burning taste, fuming

Colorless, transparent, prismatic crystals resemble MgSO₄ and ZnSO₄

Fatal Period

12–24 hours

1–2 hours (may extend to 2 days–2 weeks with renal failure)

Signs and Symptoms
  • Oropharyngeal burns, pain in throat and epigastrium
  • Dysphagia, dyspnea, dysphonia
  • Eructation, vomiting
  • Thirst
  • Fulminating: Immediate symptoms, coffee-ground vomiting, severe thirst, diarrhea, electrolyte imbalance, death within minutes
  • Acute: Tingling, numbness, tetany, convulsions, renal failure
  • Delayed: Nephritis, oxaluria, renal failure

Vomitus

Acidic, contains altered blood and mucous

Coffee-ground vomitus

Teeth

Yellowish coating, not brittle

No specific change

Urination & Tenesmus

Present

Renal stones, renal failure, scanty urine, oxaluria

Abdominal Findings
  • Abdominal distension due to gas
  • Tenderness
  • Stiffness (due to distension)

Burning pain, abdominal distension

Skin and Mucosa Erosion

Yellow discoloration over angles of mouth, lips, and fingers
  • No external findings
  • Mucosal bleaching, corrosion in mouth, esophagus, and stomach

Perforation of Stomach

Less common

No perforation, gelatinous brown content in stomach (Option D) (Option B ruled out)

Postmortem Findings

(Option A and D ruled out)
  • Yellow discoloration of skin
  • Congestion of larynx, trachea
  • Soft, friable stomach wall, ulcerated
  • Bleached mucosa (mouth, pharynx, esophagus)
  • Red, velvety, or blackish stomach wall
  • Swollen, congested kidneys with necrosis

Medico-Legal Aspects

Accidental or suicidal, homicide is rare

Usually accidental (mistaken for MgSO₄), rare in suicides or homicides, occasionally used as an abortifacient
Immediate management Dilution with water or milk if the patient is conscious Immediate calcium administration (calcium gluconate or calcium chloride)
Gastric lavage Contraindicated (risk of perforation in corrosive poisoning) Early gastric lavage with lime water or calcium solution may be used to precipitate oxalate
Specific antidote

No specific antidote

Neutralizing agent - Mild alkaline solutions (milk, antacids) to dilute acid

 Calcium gluconate/Calcium chloride - Calcium salts bind oxalic acid and form insoluble calcium oxalate
Supportive treatment Airway protection, IV fluids, analgesics, treatment of shock IV fluids, correction of hypocalcemia, management of renal failure
Complications Esophageal strictures, perforation, mediastinitis Acute kidney injury due to oxalate crystal deposition

Goutam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd Edition, Page 482, 483, 485, 486

explanationHtml:
Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive and can cause characteristic blackish burns, particularly on the mucosal surfaces, such as the lips and mouth along with chalky white, brittle

teeth. This is a key forensic finding in sulfuric acid ingestion cases.

Sulfuric Acid (H₂SO₄)

Signs and Symptoms
  • Burning sensation and pain in the throat and epigastric region.
  • Dysphagia, dyspnea, dysphonia
  • Eructation and vomiting: Frequent belching and vomiting.
  • Thirst: Present (worsened vomiting by drinking fluids)
  • Vomitus: Strongly acidic, contains altered blood and mucous shreds.
  • Teeth: Become chalky white and brittle.
  • Constipation: Usually present.
  • Urination: Suppressed.
  • Tenesmus present
  • Nature of stool: Presence of mucus and altered blood.
  • Tenderness over the abdomen
  • Abdominal stiffness due to peritonitis
  • Abdominal distension: Uncommon.
  • Skin and mucous membrane erosion: Especially on the mouth, lips, and fingers; blackening and excoriation occur.
  • Stomach Perforation: Frequently seen.

Cause of Death
  • Shock, stomach perforation, peritonitis, laryngeal spasm, and malnutrition from esophageal stricture.

Postmortem Findings
  • Erosion of skin and mouth angles, black charring of the stomach, stomach perforation, and swelling in the liver and kidneys.

Perforation of stomach

Thinning of posterior wall of the stomach

Medico-Legal Aspects
  • Often occurs accidentally (mistaken for glycerin) or in suicide cases.
  • Rarely associated with homicide.
  • May be used as an abortifacient or for vitriolage (acid attacks).


  • Bright red lividity (Option A): This is typically associated with carbon monoxide poisoning, not sulfuric acid poisoning.
  • Greenish discoloration of the skin (Option C): This is more typical of certain copper compounds, not sulfuric acid poisoning..
  • Yellowish staining and necrosis of the lips and mouth (Option D): This is typically associated with nitric acid poisoning.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Gastric lavage can be performed with caution for carbolic acid (Phenol) poisoning using lukewarm water, charcoal, olive oil, or magnesium sulfate.
  • Care is taken to prevent further absorption of the corrosive substance.
  • In oxalic acid poisoning, gastric lavage with calcium lactate (2 tsp/lavage) is done

Type of Poison

Management

Mineral Acids

(Sulphuric acid, Nitric acid, Hydrochloric acid)
  • Avoid gastric lavage/emetics.
  • Give milk or water for dilution.
  • Administer aluminum hydroxide gel (4 tbsp).
  • Provide demulcents (milk, egg white, olive oil, etc.).
  • Avoid bicarbonate/neutralizers.
  • Prednisolone 60 mg/day in divided doses.
  • Treat shock with IV fluids, blood, antibiotics (if perforation).
  • Tracheostomy for glottic edema.
  • NPO for 1 week → IV nutrition → gradual oral intake.
  • Morphine for pain; symptomatic care

Organic Acids

Oxalic Acid

  • Gastric lavage with calcium lactate (2 tsp/lavage).
  • Antidotes: Limewater, calcium lactate, calcium gluconate/chloride (150 mg/kg orally) to form insoluble calcium oxalate for excretion.
  • Calcium gluconate: 10 ml of 10% solution IV frequently.
  • Parathyroid extracts: 100 units IM.
  • Bowel management: Demulcent drinks, enemas, purgatives.
  • Hemodialysis/exchange transfusion if needed.
  • Symptomatic treatment.

Carbolic Acid (Phenol)

  • Gastric lavage (done with caution) with lukewarm water, charcoal, olive oil, MgSO4, or Na2SO4.
  • Leave medicinal liquid paraffin or 30 g MgSO4 in the stomach after lavage.
  • Provide demulcents.
  • IV saline with 7 g NaHCO3/l to manage circulatory depression, dilute carbolic acid and promote diuresis.
  • If phenol contacts the skin: Remove contaminated clothing, wash with soap and water, and apply olive oil/methylated spirit.
  • Emetics have a limited role.

Alkalis
  • Gastric lavage/emetics contraindicated.
  • Immediately dilute with water.
  • Give demulcents (egg white, milk).
  • Administer O2 inhalation in case of ammonia vapor poisoning
  • Maintain airway, tracheostomy if needed.
  • Administer parenteral analgesics and antibiotics.
  • Steroids contraindicated if esophageal perforation is present.

Note:

  • Alkali will cause liquefactive necrosis-more toxic
  • Acid will cause coagulative necrosis


Reference:

Goutam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd Edition, Page 483, 485, 487

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given plant is Digitalis Purpurea, which In toxic doses, increases cardiac excitability and causes extrasystoles.

Digitalis Purpurea (Foxglove):

Source Digitalis purpurea (Foxglove plant)
Poisonous parts Leaves, roots, and seeds
Active principles Digoxin, Digitoxin, Digitalin, Digitalein, Digitonin
Target organ Heart (cardiac muscle)

Mechanism of action
  • Inhibition of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump in cardiac myocytes, which causes increased intracellular Na⁺, which reduces the activity of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.
  • As a result, intracellular Ca²⁺ increases, leading to enhanced myocardial contractility (positive inotropic effect)
  • Digoxin also increases vagal tone, which slows AV nodal conduction

Net effects on the heart

  • Positive inotropic effect – increased cardiac contractility
  • Negative chronotropic effect – decreased heart rate
  • Negative dromotropic effect – slowed AV conduction
Mechanism of Toxicity
  • Excess intracellular calcium leads to delayed after-depolarizations, increasing myocardial excitability. This results in ectopic beats and arrhythmias, particularly extrasystoles (premature ventricular contractions).
  • Thus, the toxin in digitalis poisoning causes extrasystoles due to increased cardiac excitability.

Treatment
  • ECG monitoring
  • Gastric lavage with tannic acid solution
  • Activated charcoal
  • Purgatives if needed
  • Atropine for bradycardia
  • Potassium chloride to reduce extrasystoles
  • Lignocaine, novocaine, or propranolol for cardiac arrhythmias
  • Trisodium EDTA may help lower serum calcium
  • Specific Antidote: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digoxin immune Fab – Digibind / DigiFab)
    • These antibodies bind free digoxin in the bloodstream, forming inactive complexes that are excreted by the kidneys.
    • Indicated in life-threatening arrhythmias, severe hyperkalemia, or severe digoxin toxicity.


Reference:

Goutam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd Edition, Page 578

Aconitine, pseudo-aconitine, indaconitine, picraconitine, aconine.

Clinical Features

question: Which of the following statements on strychnine poisoning is wrong?

correctAnswer: C. Atomic absorption spectroscopy and BAL
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario presents a case of Arsenic Poisoning, which can be detected using atomic absorption spectrometry and neutron activation analysis.
  • Management involves the use of BAL (dimercaprol), while Naloxone serves as the antidote for opioid poisoning.


Mechanism of Toxicity (MOA)

  • Inhibition of sulfhydryl (-SH) containing enzymes: Inactivates key enzymes of cellular respiration
  • Inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase: Blocks oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production
  • Interference with mitochondrial enzymes: Leads to cellular energy failure
  • Binding to keratin-rich tissues: Accumulates in hair, skin, and nails causing dermatologic manifestations


Clinical Features:

  • Gastrointestinal: Severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, profuse diarrhea (“rice water stools”)
  • Skin changes: Hyperpigmentation (“raindrop pigmentation”), hyperkeratosis of palms and soles
  • Neurological: Peripheral neuropathy, paresthesia, weakness
  • Cardiovascular: Hypotension, arrhythmias in severe toxicity
  • Hematological: Anemia, leukopenia
  • Chronic exposure signs: Mee’s lines (transverse white lines on nails), skin thickening
  • Other features: Fatigue, weight loss, multisystem involvement

Investigations of Arsenic Poisoning

Tests

  • The following tests estimate the concentration of arsenic in hair, bone, and nails:
  • Neutron activation analysis (NAA) (Option A)
  • Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) (Option C)
  • The following tests are obsolete now:
    • Marsh test (Option B)
    • Reinsch test
    • Gutzeit test (Option D)

Urine levels

>50 microns in 24 hours indicates arsenic poisoning (Best)

Blood level

Serum arsenic > 0.9 µg/dl

Hair level

Best sample: Pubic hair (used for long-term exposure detection).

Radiography

Abdominal X-ray: May show arsenic presence in the gastrointestinal tract in cases of acute poisoning.


Management of Arsenic Poisoning

Supportive treatment

Gastric lavage, airway, breathing, and circulation management (intravenous fluids, cardiac monitoring, etc.).

Medical treatment

Freshly prepared hydrated ferric oxide (chemical antidote)

Chelating agents
  • BAL (Dimercaprol) (Option C)
  • DMSA (Dimercapto succinic acid) or DMPS (Dimercapto propane sulfonic acid)
  • Penicillamine

Other measures
  • Purgatives like Castor oil or Magnesium sulfate (remove unabsorbed poison from the intestine).
  • Glucose-saline with sodium bicarbonate.
  • Hemodialysis or exchange transfusion.


Reference:
  1. Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Pages 408-410
  2. Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, Pages 490, 491
  3. Modern Medical Toxicology, by VV Pillai, 4th Edition, Pages 79-82

Methanol Poisoning

Wood Alcohol/ Illicit Alcohol
Hooch Tragedy

Wernicke's encephalopathy is characterised by a triad of Disorientation, ophthalmoplegia, and polyneuropathy (ataxia) due to thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, commonly seen in chronic alcoholics.

Chronic Alcoholism Manifestations

Wernicke's Encephalopathy
  • Caused by Thiamine Deficiency
  • Mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, periaqueductal gray, floor of 4th ventricle are affected
  • Symptoms
    • Global confusion, ataxia and Apathy (early symptoms)
    • Polyneuropathy
    • Ophthalmoplegia
    • Disorientation, recent memory loss and loss of attention span
  • Rx - IV Thiamine followed by oral thiamine.

Korsakoff Psychosis (Option C)
  • Caused by untreated Wernicke's Encephalopathy
  • Mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial nucleus of the thalamus are affected
  • Symptoms
    • Confabulation
    • Retrograde and Anterograde Amnesia
    • Difficulty in learning new things
    • Severe Disorientation.
  • Rx - IV Thiamine followed by oral thiamine

MarChiafava's Syndrome (Option B)
  • Corpus callosum (especially body and splenium) is degenrated
  • Symptoms
    • Intellectual Disorientation
    • Epilepsy,
    • Ataxia
    • Dysarthria
    • Hallucinations
    • Spastic paralysis of the limb
    • Dementia
  • Rx: Thiamine supplementation (especially in alcohol-related cases), antiepileptic drugs for seizures, and supportive therapies like physical and speech therapy for motor and speech deficits.

Alcohol Paranoia

Paranoid delusions are present with no hallucinations

Mallory Weiss Syndrome (Option A)

It involves tears in the esophageal mucosa caused by severe vomiting or retching, which can lead to gastrointestinal bleeding and mediastinitis.

    • C = A/ PR = 100g/ 1,00,000g x 0.68 = 100/ 68000 g/ml = 0.00147 g/ml.
    • 0.00147 g/ml = 0.00147/ 100 g% = 0.147 g% = 0.147/1000 mg% = 147 mg%
  • Widmark’s Formula is widely used in Blood alcohol analysis for multiple purposes using the type of alcohol, Sex of the person and body weight.
  • The widmark formula for Urine = ¾ PCR
  • Blood is the commonly used means to calculate the level of alcohol consumption and intoxication, other than Breath, Urine, and Saliva.
  • Preservatives used while collecting blood are
    • Sodium fluoride
    • Potassium oxalate

question:
A 32-year-old male weighing 100 kg was arrested for disorderly conduct at a market. Upon questioning, he confesses to consuming 100 grams of alcohol. Using the Widmark formula, calculate his Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC).

(The Widmark constant for men is 0.68)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the second phase of intoxication, i.e. Stage of Incoordination, the BAC is usually between 150 mg% to 250 mg%.

Stages of intoxication

Stages

BAC in mg%

Symptoms

Excitement

30 - 150
  • There is slight impairment in the cognitive, sensory and motor functions at 30 mg%
  • Impaired reaction time at 50 mg%
  • Alcohol gaze nystagmus, low pain sensitivity, and poor concentration at 80 - 100mg%
  • Nausea and slight movement incoordination is seen from 100 - 150 mg%

Incoordination

150 - 250
  • Nausea and Vomiting
  • Sensory, Fine, and Skilled motor impairment
  • Elevated heart rate
  • Flushed face

[[figure-1]]

Coma

> 300
  • Markedly affected speech (Thick and slurred speech), as well as sensory and motor functions.
  • Extreme dizziness and a sense of fall are present.
  • Positive McEwan’s sign: The patient's pupils are contracted, which dilate on a stimulus like a pinch or a slap and later return to the contracted phase.

question: A 28 year old male was brought to the ED after multiple episodes of vomiting, confusion, and irritability following alcohol consumption at a party. He had a flushed face, sensory impairment, and a heart rate of 105. He was suspected to be in the 2nd phase of intoxication. What is the likely blood alcohol concentration (BAC)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario suggests features consistent with the abuse of "Love Boat," which refers to Cannabis dipped in Phencyclidine (PCP).


Source

Synthesised from piperazine, cyclohexanone, and potassium cyanide

Street names

Angel dust.

Mode of intake

Smoking; Insufflation; Ingestion; Parenteral (rare)

Combination

  • Mixed with parsley, mint, oregano, or marijuana.
  • Tragic magico: Crack (cocaine) is dipped in PCP and smoked
  • Love boat: Cannabis is dipped in PCP and smoked.

Mechanism

Blocking NMDA receptor-mediated neurotransmission and presynaptic monoamine reuptake, increasing dopamine and noradrenaline synaptic levels.

Clinical features

  • Acute psychosis & agitation:

  • PCP: Confusion, disorientation, amnesia, catatonia, dystonia, mydriasis, tachycardia, hallucinations, nystagmus, blurred vision.

  • Cannabis: Euphoria, disorientation, hallucinations, sedation/dysphoria, tachycardia, palpitations, hypotension, increased appetite.

Management

Supportive Care:

  • Sedation: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam/diazepam) for agitation, anxiety, seizures; avoid antipsychotics.

  • Hydration & Renal Support: IV fluids to maintain hydration and protect kidneys, especially with myoglobinuria or acute renal failure.

Hemlock (Option A): Hemlock (Conium maculatum) contains coniine, a neurotoxin that causes neuromuscular paralysis. Typical features include muscle weakness, ascending paralysis, respiratory failure, and eventually death due to respiratory paralysis. It does not produce agitation, hallucinations, or aggressive psychotic behaviour, making it inconsistent with the scenario.


Chloral Hydrate (Option B): Chloral hydrate is a sedative-hypnotic drug historically used for insomnia and sedation. Toxicity produces CNS depression, drowsiness, confusion, respiratory depression, hypotension, and coma. Patients are usually sedated or obtunded, not agitated or aggressive, so this option does not match the presentation.


Cocaine (Option C): Although cocaine can cause tachycardia, mydriasis, agitation, and tactile hallucinations, it usually produces stimulant toxicity with paranoia and euphoria, whereas PCP intoxication is more strongly associated with severe confusion, violent aggression, dissociative behaviour, and nystagmus.


Feature Cocaine PCP
Behaviour Euphoria, agitation, paranoia Extreme aggression, violent behaviour, dissociation
Hallucinations Often tactile hallucinations (formication – “cocaine bugs”) Severe psychosis with confusion and disorientation
Eye findings Mydriasis Characteristic nystagmus
Pain perception Normal Marked analgesia and reduced pain perception
Mental state Stimulant intoxication Dissociative delirium with confusion and amnesia

question: A 30 year old male is brought to the emergency department by friends after acting erratically in public, hallucinating, and showing aggressive behaviour. He is agitated and confused and has dilated pupils and a rapid heart rate. While his vital signs are stable, he becomes more aggressive when approached. Which substance might be abused in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The symptoms described, including hallucinations, paranoia, and severe agitation, are commonly associated with a "bad trip" on LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide).

Lysergic acid diethylamide

Source

Claviceps purpurea or rye fungus (ergot alkaloid).

[[figure-1]]

Sold as

  • Acid blotter
  • Paper stamp
  • Tiny tablets (microdots)
  • Gelatin squares (window panes)
  • Liquid or powder

[[figure-2]]

Mode

Oral intake; Smoke (rare); Parenteral (rare)

Mechanism

5HT-1 receptor agonist (increases serotonin level)

Fatal dose

14 mg

Clinical manifestations
  • Good trip: Psychotropic effect consisting of euphoria including visual hallucinations, illusions, sensations of synesthesia (seeing smell or hearing colours)
  • Bad trip: Psychotropic effect consisting of an acute panic reaction as paranoid delusion, violent behaviour, anxiety, automatism, or depersonalisation.
  • Symptoms like sweating, dry mouth, mydriasis, hypertension, tachycardia, mood change, etc.
  • Bizarre perceptual changes: Faces and body parts appear distorted, objects undulate, sounds may be amplified and distorted, and colours seem brighter with halos around them.
  • Flashback phenomenon: The individual experiences a recurrence of the emotional and psychological aspects from the previous LSD trip.

Management

  • Anti-anxiety drugs (Low dose)
  • Benzodiazepines (Diazepam)
  • Prolonged talking involves verbal reassurance to keep the person grounded and reduce paranoia.
  • Psychotherapy

question: A 25 year old male presents to the emergency department exhibiting severe agitation, hallucinations, and a heightened sense of paranoia after attending a rave. He reports feelings of overwhelming anxiety and visual distortions, claiming he sees colours and shapes that aren't there. Based on his symptoms, which substance is most likely responsible for his bad trip?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The case is diagnosed as severe acute lead poisoning with encephalopathy, where BAL (Dimercaprol) is administered immediately alongside supportive measures.

Acute Lead Poisoning
Onset Usually occurs after sudden ingestion or inhalation of large amounts of lead (industrial exposure, contaminated food/water, accidental ingestion). Acute episodes may also occur as exacerbations of chronic lead poisoning.
Early Symptoms Metallic/astringent taste, dry throat, intense thirst, malaise, headache, irritability
Gastrointestinal Features Burning abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps
Neurological Manifestations Lead encephalopathy (more common in children): irritability, delirium, seizures, confusion, coma
Cardiovascular Features Peripheral circulatory collapse, hypotension, tachycardia
Neuromuscular Features Paresthesia, muscle weakness, tremors
Severe Toxicity Convulsions, severe encephalopathy, respiratory depression, coma, death
Blood Lead Level (BLL) Markedly elevated (often >70 µg/dL in severe poisoning)
Hematological Findings

Early hemolysis or anemia; basophilic stippling may appear

[[figure-1]]
Biochemical Markers ↑ Delta-ALA, ↑ free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, ↑ zinc protoporphyrin
Urinary Findings ↑ urinary lead, coproporphyrin, and ALA
Radiology

Bone changes are usually absent initially in acute poisoning (lead lines occur in chronic exposure)

[[figure-2]]

Management of Acute Lead Poisoning

Severe acute poisoning with encephalopathy

  • BAL or Dimercaprol (administered immediately) (Option D)
  • CaNa2EDTA (calcium disodium edetate) (contraindicated in renal failure)
  • For Cerebral edema:
    • Mannitol
    • Furosemide
    • Corticosteroids (Dexamethasone)
  • Continue until the patient is asymptomatic, then start oral chelation (D-penicillamine or DMSA).

Severe acute poisoning without encephalopathy

(Blood Lead level >70 mcg/100 ml)

  • BAL
  • EDTA
  • When BL <40 mcg/100 ml
    • Discontinue BAL
    • Continue EDTA
    • Change to oral chelation (D-penicillamine or DMSA).

Moderate poisoning

(Blood Lead level: 45-70 mcg/100 ml)
  • EDTA
  • When BL <40 mcg/100ml: Oral chelation (D-penicillamine or DMSA)

Mild poisoning

(Blood Lead level: 20-35 mcg/100 ml)
  • D-penicillamine (Option C) or
  • DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) (Option B)

Supportive measures
  • Thiamine
  • Calcium gluconate (Option A)
  • Magnesium sulphate
  • DMSA (succimer)
  • BAL (dimercaprol) and EDTA are used together because EDTA can redistribute lead to the brain, while BAL helps to prevent this redistribution.

question: A 35 year old man who works in a jewelry factory is brought to the emergency department drowsy, with sudden irritability, confusion, and vomiting over 24 hours. Examination shows a bluish line on his gums and pallor, and blood tests confirm acute heavy metal poisoning with cerebral oedema on the CT scan. Along with maintenance ofairway, breathing, and circulation, what is the immediate management?

correctAnswer: C. Blood lead level &gt;40 micrograms/100 ml
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Blood lead level >40 micrograms/100 ml is the definitive diagnostic criterion for lead poisoning, indicating significant exposure requiring intervention.
  • Microcytic-hypochromic anaemia with basophilic stippling (Option A), Increased urinary Coproporphyrin (Option B), and Free Erythrocyte Protoporphyrin (FEP) (Option C) are indicators of lead exposure or impaired heme synthesis but are not definitive diagnostic markers.


Laboratory findings of Lead poisoning:

Blood analysis

CBC and Peripheral Blood Smear
  • Microcytic-hypochromic anemia
  • Anisocytosis
  • Poikilocytosis and Polycythemia
  • Basophilic stippling (Option B) and Cabot rings in RBCs

Blood lead levels (BL)
  • >5 microgram/ 100 ml (lead exposure)
  • >40 micrograms (appearance of signs and symptoms)

ZnP (Zinc Protoporphyrin) levels

35-50 microgram/ 100 ml.

FEP (Free Erythrocyte Protoporphyrin)

Elevated

Urine analysis

ALA (Amino Levulinic Acid) levels

>5 micrograms/L

Urinary coproporphyrin level

>150 mcg /litre

Urine lead level

0.25 milligram/ litre

Calcium disodium EDTA mobilisation test

This test is primarily conducted in children to determine whether they will respond to chelation therapy with a significant lead diuresis.

Clinical manifestations

Facial pallor

It is caused by vasospasm and specifically occurs circumorally, which is the earliest and most specific feature.

Lead line or Burtonian lines

The stippled blue line observed on the gums, resulting from a subepithelial deposit of granules that develops within one week, is seen in 50-70% of cases and is more common in individuals with carious teeth (bacteria form lead sulfide).

Lead osteopathy/Lead line (Bone-line)

In children, calcium deposition occurs at the growth plates of bones (specifically the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia), which appears as a radiopaque band and occurs over 4 weeks due to the inhibition of osteoclastic activity.

Colic and constipation

(Painter's Colic or Devonshire colic)

Late presentation occurs in 85% of cases, typically at night, and is characterised by spasmodic pain relieved by pressure

Lead palsy

Predominantly motor features include:

  • Dry bellyache
  • Wrist drop (Radial nerve)

  • Foot drop (Common peroneal nerve)

Encephalopathy

This condition is seen in nearly all cases, is associated with tetraethyl lead exposure, primarily affects children, results in permanent brain damage in 85% of cases, and accounts for 25% of fatalities

Reproductive system
  • Amenorrhea
  • Dysmenorrhea
  • Abortion
  • Sterility derangements (both sexes)

Cardiovascular system and Kidneys
  • Hypertension (vascular constriction)
  • Permanent arteriolar degeneration
  • Nephritis

Gout

Saturnine gout (due to decreased excretion of uric acid)

Others

These include generalised weakness, anorexia, dyspepsia, emaciation, exhaustion, irritability, foul breath, headache, vertigo, alopecia, and dizziness.



Reference:
  1. Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 412. 413
  2. Modern Medical Toxicology, by VV Pillai, 4th Edition, Pages 87, 88

question: A 5-year-old child presents with developmental delay, irritability, and abdominal pain. Laboratory investigations for lead poisoning are ordered. Which of the following is the definitive indicator of lead poisoning?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The described scenario, with symptoms and an image showing circumoral pallor, indicates lead poisoning. In this condition, Burton's lines, basophilic stippling, and calcium deposition at bone ends are observed, while phossy jaw (seen in phosphorus poisoning) is absent.


Acute lead poisoning

  • It’s rare, and there may be exacerbations of chronic lead poisoning.
  • Symptoms: Astringent or metallic taste, dry throat, thirst, burning abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, peripheral circulatory collapse, paraesthesia, depression, coma, and death.



Chronic lead poisoning (Plumbism or Saturnism)

Clinical manifestations

Facial pallor

It is caused by vasospasm and specifically occurs circumorally, which is the earliest and most specific feature.

Anemia
  • Type: Microcytic-hypochromic.
  • Enzymes inhibited:
    • Ferrochelatase
    • ALA-dehydratase
    • Coproporphyrinogen oxidase
  • Blood picture:
    • Cabot rings in RBCs
    • Microcytic-hypochromic
    • Sideroblasts (nucleated red cells)
    • Anisocytosis
    • Poikilocytosis
    • Polycythemia

Basophilic stippling or Punctate basophilia (Option B)
  • Multiple blue-coloured pinhead dots in RBCs due to the toxic action of lead on porphyrin metabolism (inhibition of enzyme 5- Pyrimidine nucleotidase) (PNN).
  • Accumulation of ribosomes in RBC

Lead line or Burtonian lines (Option A)

The stippled blue line observed on the gums, resulting from a subepithelial deposit of granules that develops within one week, is seen in 50-70% of cases and is more common in individuals with carious teeth (bacteria form lead sulfide).

Lead osteopathy/Lead line (Bone-line) (Option D)

In children, calcium deposition occurs at the growth plates of bones (specifically the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia), which appears as a radiopaque band and occurs over 4 weeks due to the inhibition of osteoclastic activity.

Colic and constipation

(Painter's Colic or Devonshire colic)

Late presentation occurs in 85% of cases, typically at night, and is characterised by spasmodic pain relieved by pressure.

Lead palsy

Predominantly motor features include:

  • Dry belly ache
  • Wrist drop (Radial nerve)

  • Foot drop (Common peroneal nerve)

Encephalopathy

This condition is seen in nearly all cases, is associated with tetraethyl lead exposure, primarily affects children, results in permanent brain damage in 85% of cases, and accounts for 25% of fatalities.

Reproductive system
  • Amenorrhea
  • Dysmenorrhea
  • Abortion
  • Sterility derangements (both sexes)

Cardiovascular system and Kidneys
  • Hypertension (vascular constriction)
  • Permanent arteriolar degeneration
  • Nephritis

Gout

Saturnine gout (due to decreased excretion of uric acid)

Others

These include generalised weakness, anorexia, dyspepsia, emaciation, exhaustion, irritability, foul breath, headache, vertigo, alopecia, and dizziness.

Diagnosis & Management

Key Enzymes Inhibited ALA-dehydratase, Ferrochelatase, Coproporphyrinogen oxidase, Pyrimidine nucleotidase
Laboratory findings– Blood Lead Level (BLL) Elevated (>5 µg/dL abnormal in children; >45 µg/dL → chelation therapy)
Peripheral Blood Findings Microcytic hypochromic anemia, basophilic stippling, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis
Biochemical Markers ↑ Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP), ↑ Zinc protoporphyrin, ↑ urinary ALA, and coproporphyrin
Radiology X-ray long bones → Radiopaque metaphyseal lead lines (distal femur, proximal tibia)
Urine Findings Increased lead excretion after chelation
Initial Management Remove source of exposure (paint, contaminated dust, batteries, industrial exposure)
Chelation Therapy
  • Succimer (DMSA) – oral drug of choice in moderate poisoning (especially children)
  • Calcium disodium EDTA – parenteral chelator for moderate–severe poisoning
  • Dimercaprol (BAL) – used with EDTA in severe poisoning with encephalopathy
  • Penicillamine – alternative chelating agent
Supportive Management Treat seizures, maintain hydration, correct anemia, nutritional support (iron, calcium)



Phossy jaw (Option C), also known as glass jaw or Lucifer’s jaw, refers to osteonecrosis of the jawbone. This condition is associated with phosphorus poisoning.

question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the paediatrician due to irritability, decreased appetite, abdominal pain, and difficulty concentrating. She exhibits signs of anaemia and pallor, as depicted in the image below. Blood tests confirm heavy metal poisoning. Which clinical manifestations are not typically associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario, featuring symptoms such as irritability, stomach pain, and the presence of blue gum lines (Burtonian lines), indicates chronic lead poisoning. The image shows basophilic stippling, a characteristic haematological finding in lead toxicity.

[[figure-1]]

Hematological manifestations of Lead poisoning:

  • Microcytic-Hypochromic Anemia
  • Basophilic Stippling
  • Anisocytosis
  • Poikilocytosis
  • Elevated Free Erythrocyte Protoporphyrin (FEP)
  • Increased Zinc Protoporphyrin (ZnP)

Target cells (Option A) are characterised by a central area of haemoglobin encircled by a pale ring, creating a target-like appearance. They are seen in liver disease, thalassemia, haemoglobin C disease, and post-splenectomy.

[[figure-2]]

Spherocytes (Option C) are dense cells lacking central pallor, seen in conditions like autoimmune hemolytic anaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, and post-splenectomy.

[[figure-3]]

Rouleaux formation (Option D) is the sticking together of red blood cells in linear arrays, commonly caused by high blood M protein levels. It is seen in various conditions, such as multiple myeloma, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), malaria, and HIV.

question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for irritability, poor appetite, and stomach pain. The family recently moved into an old house that is under renovation. Examination reveals pallor and a blue line on the gums. Blood smear findings are noted. What is the most likely finding on the blood smear in this child with suspected lead poisoning?

correctAnswer: C. Ingestion of lead dust or paint chips
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most common route of childhood lead exposure is ingestion of lead paint chips or lead-contaminated household dust.

  • Older homes with deteriorating lead-based paint shed flakes and fine dust into the environment.

  • Children frequently play on floors and surfaces where this dust accumulates.

  • Natural hand-to-mouth behavior causes them to ingest significant amounts unintentionally.

  • Lead dust also settles on toys, furniture, and objects that children put in their mouths.

  • Young children absorb a much higher fraction of ingested lead compared to adults.

  • Thus, ingestion of lead dust/paint chips remains the primary and most important exposure pathway in pediatric lead poisoning.

Incorrect Options:

Option A) Inhalation of lead-contaminated air: This route is more important in occupational or industrial settings (battery factories, smelting, welding). Environmental air levels are usually too low to cause significant poisoning in children. Not the primary route in household exposure.

Option B) Ingestion of lead-contaminated water: Can occur through lead plumbing or pipes, but this is far less common than ingestion of lead dust/paint chips. Water usually contributes a smaller percentage of total lead burden in children.

Option D) Absorption through skin: Lead is not significantly absorbed through intact skin, especially in inorganic forms (the usual household type). Therefore, dermal exposure does not contribute meaningfully to lead toxicity in children.



Reference:

Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page 412.

Modern Medical Toxicology, by VV Pillai, 4th Edition, Page, 83, 84.

question: A 6 year old girl was brought to the clinic by her parents, who reported symptoms including irritability, stomach pain, difficulty concentrating, decreased appetite, and fatigue. The examination showed signs of anaemia and facial circumoral pallor, leading the doctor to suspect heavy metal poisoning. What is the most common route of exposure to this poison in children?

correctAnswer: B. Blocks RNA polymerase, preventing protein synthesis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario and given image suggest ingestion of Ricinus seeds,
  • The toxic principle in castor seeds is ricin, a highly toxic toxalbumin.
  • Ricin consists of two polypeptide chains (A and B) linked by a disulfide bond.
    • Chain B binds to the cell surface and facilitates entry of the toxin into the cell.
    • Chain A disrupts protein synthesis by acting on the 60S ribosomal subunit.
  • Inhibition of protein synthesis leads to cell death and the toxic manifestations of ricin poisoning.

[[figure-1]]

  • Clinical Features:
    • Symptoms usually begin after a delay of several hours.
    • Initial features:
      • Burning sensation in the GI tract
      • Colicky abdominal pain
      • Vomiting
      • Bloody diarrhea and tenesmus
    • Severe poisoning:
      • Hemorrhagic gastritis
      • Dehydration and shock
    • Systemic Toxicity:
      • CNS: Delayed cranial nerve toxicity; optic nerve damage reported.
      • Kidneys: Hematuria, ↑ creatinine, acute renal failure.
      • Liver: Hepatic injury in severe cases.
  • Toxic Dose:
    • Whole seeds are usually harmless because the hard coat resists digestion.
    • Toxicity occurs when seeds are crushed or chewed, releasing ricin.
    • Generally, 8-10 seeds are required for fatal poisoning, though even a single seed may rarely cause fatal anaphylaxis.
    • Toxic effects may take up to 5 days to fully manifest.
  • Treatment:
    • Observe for at least 8 hours after significant exposure.
    • Decontamination: Gastric lavage, activated charcoal, catharsis.
    • Supportive care: IV fluids and monitoring for hypovolemia and organ dysfunction.
    • No specific antidote is available.

Inhibits calcium ion channels, causing cell death (Option A): Ricin does not act on calcium channels; its toxicity results from inhibition of protein synthesis.

Blocks RNA polymerase, preventing protein synthesis (Option B): Ricin does not inhibit RNA polymerase or transcription; it acts at the ribosomal level.

Disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to energy failure (Option D): Ricin does not primarily affect mitochondria; its main mechanism is inhibition of protein synthesis via the 60S ribosomal subunit.



Reference:

Gautam Biswas Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 3rd Edition, Pages 517,518

question: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department after ingesting the seeds given in the image. He has severe abdominal pain, bloody vomiting, dizziness, and a rapid, weak pulse. What is the mechanism of action of the toxic compound present in the seeds?

correctAnswer: A. Rigor mortis sets in quickly

Postmortem findings of Arsenic Poisoning

External findings

Internal findings

  • Raindrop pigmentation
  • Keratosis
  • Alopecia
  • White streaks on nails (Aldrich Mees’ lines)

question: A 28 year old man is brought to the emergency department in an altered mental state after reportedly using a speedball for a more intense high. His friends mention he often combines a powerful stimulant with another drug to enhance his experience. What is the composition of a speedball that he is likely using?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cardiac arrhythmia is a fatal complication of cocaine use.

Cocaine

Origin

Leaves of Erythroxylum coca

[[figure-1]]

Signs of abuse
  • Septal perforation
  • Crack hands (multiple blackened, hyperkeratotic lesions on the fingers and palms).
  • Black staining of tongue and teeth

Effects

Stages:

1. Stage of Excitement:

  • Sense of well-being

  • Loss of fatigue and depression

  • Restlessness and excitement

  • Tingling in hands and feet

  • Increased heart rate and temperature

  • Rapid, deep respiration

2. Stage of Depression:

  • Profuse sweating

  • Convulsions

  • Decreased respiratory rate

Complications

  • Cardiac arrhythmia (Option B)
  • Cardiac failure
  • Cardiovascular collapse
  • Cerebrovascular accident
  • Aortic dissection
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Skin necrosis
  • Intracerebral hemorrhage
  • Formication (Cocaine Bugs)

Management of fatal dose
  • Maintain airway, breathing and circulation
  • If ingested: Gastric lavage with potassium permanganate
  • If snorted: Wash the nasal mucous membrane with water
  • If injected: Ligature over the injection site
  • Amyl nitrite via inhalation route
  • Thiamine 100 mg IV injection
  • Naloxone hydrochloride 2mg IV injection

Respiratory depression (Option A) is a complication that is often associated with the use of opium, alcohol, barbiturates, and benzodiazepine. Cocaine is a stimulant, and it does not cause respiratory depression.

Urinary retention (Option C) is a complication that can occur in cases of datura/atropine poisoning. The patient has a dry mouth, dysphagia, delirium, a dilated pupil, urinary retention, respiratory paralysis, and dry skin.

• Lead is a toxic substance that can be released from retained lead bullets, especially if the bullet is lodged in the body for a prolonged period. Lead gradually leaches into the bloodstream and can cause neurological issues (e.g., confusion, memory problems, and in extreme cases, encephalopathy), kidney damage, gastrointestinal symptoms, and anemia.

Causes of Chronic Lead Poisoning:

  1. Ingestion or Inhalation of lead-containing dust.: Most common source
  2. Lead Paint Dust:
    • Major source for children, especially those under 3 years old.
    • Children are at greater risk due to pica (eating non-nutritive materials).
  3. Inhalation by Occupational Exposure: Workers in industries such as white lead manufacturing, lead paint production, plumbing, glass polishing, printing, and glass blowing are at risk.
  4. Contaminated Drinking Water: Absorption of lead from water stored in lead cisterns.
  5. Lead in Tinned Food
  6. Cosmetics and Hair Dyes
  7. Petrol and Gasoline: Percutaneous absorption of tetraethyl lead
  8. Lead absorption from vermilion (red pigment) used on the scalp.
  9. Lead poisoning can result from retained lead bullets or projectiles lodged in the body.

Iron (Option A): Not related to retained bullets. Iron poisoning typically occurs from ingesting large amounts of iron and affects the gastrointestinal system, liver, and kidneys.

Phosphorus (Option B): Occurs from exposure to white phosphorus and causes damage to the liver, but not associated with retained bullets.

Nitrocellulose (Option C): Found in gunpowder, but it does not cause poisoning from retained bullets.

explanationHtml:
• Cyanide poisoning (HCN) causes pink skin and mucosa, bitter almond odor from the breath, and frothy discharge, which are key diagnostic clues. It is caused by the exposure to hydrogen cyanide (HCN) or cyanide salts. Cyanide interferes with cellular respiration by inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase, an enzyme in the mitochondria, leading to histotoxic anoxia (cells cannot use oxygen, even when it is available in the bloodstream).

Cyanide poisoning

Physical Appearance
  • Gaseous state- Hydrogen cyanide (HCN)
  • Liquid form- Hydrocyanic acid or Prussic acid
  • Solid state- salt forms

Sources of poisoning
  • Electroplating, photographic processes, rubber, and plastic manufacturing industries
  • Insecticide and rodenticide
  • Drug toxicity: Sodium nitroprusside
  • Military chemical warfare agents
  • Burning of plastic furniture, silk, or wool
  • Cigarette smoking
  • Bitter almonds, peach, apricot, plum, apple, pear, cassava

Mode of Action
  • Rapid absorption across both skin and mucous membrane
  • Cyanide salts combine with hydrochloric acid in the stomach to form HCN that is absorbed
  • Inhibition of cytochrome oxidase causes histotoxic anoxia
  • Neurotoxicity

Clinical Features
  • Inhalation: Dizziness, vertigo, and constriction of the throat
  • Ingestion: Nausea, headache, loss of muscular power, hypotension, cardiovascular failure, and convulsion
  • Skin: Brick-red color of skin and mucous membranes
  • Anion gap metabolic acidosis and lactic acidosis

Diagnosis
  • Lee-Jones test
  • Serum cyanide level

Treatment
  • Severe acidosis (pH < 7.1): Administer sodium bicarbonate
  • Antidotal therapy (Eli Lilly cyanide kit approach)
    • First step: Inhalation of Amyl nitrite
    • Second step: Sodium nitrite (3% solution) IV
    • Third step: Sodium thiosulfate (25% solution) IV
  • Other Antidotes
    • 4-dimethylaminophenol (4-DMAP)
    • Hydroxocobalamin (Vitamin B12): Combines with cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in the urine
    • Hyperbaric oxygen
  • Note: Methylene blue is NOT an antidote for cyanide and must NOT be used

Autopsy Findings
  • Bitter almond’s odour
  • Brick-red color of skin and mucous membranes
  • Cyanosis of extremities
  • Hemorrhagic gastritis
  • Disseminated petechiae in brain, meninges, pleura, lungs, and pericardium
  • Pulmonary and cerebral edema

Note:

  • Mechanism of action of nitrites: It converts hemoglobin to methemoglobinemia which causes the detachment of cyanide from the heme group of cytochrome oxidase.
  • Mechanism of action of sodium thiosulfate: Forms non-toxic thiocyanate which is excreted in the urine.

H2S poisoning (Option A): Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) poisoning typically presents with rotten egg smell from the breath, not the bitter almond smell seen in cyanide poisoning. Symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and in severe cases, respiratory failure. The skin typically does not have the pink color seen in cyanide poisoning.

CO poisoning (Option B): Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning leads to a cherry-red skin color, not pink as seen in cyanide poisoning. The breath does not have a bitter almond smell, and the classic symptoms are headache, dizziness, confusion, and weakness, not frothy discharge.

OPC poisoning (Option D): Organophosphate (OP) poisoning typically presents with symptoms such as muscarinic effects (e.g., excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, gastrointestinal distress) and nicotinic effects (muscle weakness, paralysis). The skin does not have a characteristic pink color, and there is no bitter almond odor from the breath. Frothy discharge is not a typical symptom of OPC poisoning.



Reference:

Modern Medical Toxicology VV Pillay, 4th Edition- Page 364-69.

explanationHtml:
• The symptoms of pinpoint pupils (miosis) and increased secretions (such as salivation, lacrimation, and bronchorrhea) are highly suggestive of organophosphorus poisoning. Organophosphates inhibit cholinesterase enzymes, leading to the accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.

Symptoms

Muscarinic: Lethargy, Salivation, Diarrhea, Lacrimation, Urination, Miosis, Muscle weakness, Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia, Emesis (Mnemonic: DUMBBELLS)

Nicotinic: Muscle weakness, Fasciculation, Areflexia, Muscle paralysis

CNS: Headache, Tremor, Confusion, Slurred speech, Coma, Convulsion

Laboratory Diagnosis
  • RBC/True Cholinesterase (specific)
  • Plasma/Pseudocholinesterase (Most common)
    • Falls rapidly with organophosphorus poisoning
    • Inexpensive, sensitive)
  • Atropine test: If 2 mg of Atropine relieves symptoms, it confirms OP poisoning
  • P-nitro phenol test for confirmation.

Management
  • Resuscitative measures (Airway-Breathing-Circulation)
  • Decontamination
  • Gastric lavage with 1:5000 KMnO4
  • Activated charcoal
  • Atropine sulfate (2-4 mg IV every 10-15 minutes until atropinization)
  • Signs of atropinization: Heart rate>80 beats/min, pupils no longer pinpoint, clear chest on auscultation with no wheeze, systolic BP>80mmHg, Dry axillae
  • Oximes (Pralidoxime) to decrease muscarinic and CNS symptoms
    • removes phosphate group
    • reduces atropine requirement

Cause of Death

Respiratory Muscle Paralysis (RMP)

[[figure-1]]

Alcohol poisoning (Option A): Alcohol typically causes CNS depression, but does not cause pinpoint pupils or excessive secretions

Opioid poisoning (Option B): Opioids cause miosis (pinpoint pupils) but do not cause excessive secretions or the broad range of symptoms seen in organophosphorus poisoning.\

Datura poisoning (Option D): Datura causes mydriasis (dilated pupils) and other anticholinergic symptoms like dry mouth, blurred vision, and tachycardia, which are opposite to the muscarinic symptoms caused by organophosphorus poisoning.



Reference:

Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 3rd Edition, PG,597-600

• Huffing involves inhaling the vapors of an inhalant, typically from a cloth or rag soaked in volatile solvents.
  • It is a method where the substance is directly inhaled through the mouth, and a cloth soaked in the drug is commonly used for this method.
  • Inhalants are substances that produce intoxicating vapors when inhaled, often used by young adolescents.
  • They can cause severe health issues, including cardiac arrest, suffocation, and long-term damage to the brain, heart, kidneys, and liver.

Types of Inhalants:

  1. Volatile Solvents: Liquids that vaporize at room temperature, found in household and business products like paint thinners, dry-cleaning fluids, gasoline, glues, and felt-tip markers.
  2. Aerosols: Products that release vapors when sprayed, such as spray paints, deodorant sprays, hair sprays, and cooking oil sprays.
  3. Gases: Gases like nitrous oxide (laughing gas), chloroform, ether, and halothane, used in medical procedures. Also includes gases found in butane lighters, propane tanks, and refrigerants.
  4. Nitrites: Sold in small bottles called “poppers,” these primarily dilate blood vessels and relax muscles, acting differently from other inhalants that affect the central nervous system.

Bagging (Option A): This involves inhaling vapors from a substance stored in a plastic bag. It is a common method of inhaling gases or solvents but does not specifically refer to inhaling a cloth soaked in a drug.

Spraying (Option B): This refers to inhaling vapors directly from an aerosol or spray can, such as spray paints or deodorant sprays. It is a method of inhaling aerosol inhalants, but it does not apply to inhaling from a cloth soaked in a drug.

Sniffing (Option D): This involves inhaling vapors directly from a container or surface, such as sniffing glue or other substances. However, it does not specifically refer to inhaling from a cloth soaked in a drug.

• In forensic autopsies, the stomach is usually opened along the greater curvature to minimize disruption of stomach anatomy and allows the pathologist to collect and examine the stomach contents effectively, which is critical in cases of suspected poisoning.

Procedure for Stomach Dissection:

  1. Two ligatures are applied at the cardiac end of the esophagus and two ligatures are below the pyloric end of the stomach.
  2. The stomach is removed by cutting between the double ligatures at both ends.
  3. The stomach is then opened along the greater curvature.
  4. The mucous membrane is examined for the presence of any stains, congestion, hemorrhage, desquamation, ulceration, sloughing, or perforation.
  5. The contents of the stomach are noted with respect to quantity, nature of material/food, state of digestion, color, and smell.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Gastric Lavage in Poisoning Management

[[figure-1]]

  • Gastric lavage is a procedure to remove ingested poison by introducing and withdrawing fluids through an orogastric tube. Its effectiveness depends on timing, proper technique, and patient-specific considerations.

Timing and Effectiveness

  • Most effective within 1 hour of ingestion
  • Can be beneficial up to 4-6 hours in select cases
  • Beyond 6 hours, poison likely passes into the intestines, reducing lavage efficacy

Procedure Steps

Step

Details

Patient Positioning

Trendelenburg: Head down to prevent aspiration

Left lateral decubitus: Reduces chance of poison entering the duodenum

Tube Placement Confirmation

Inject air and listen for gastric bubbling sounds

Watch for coughing or bubbles (indicates misplacement in trachea)

Fluid Administration

Fluid is administered and aspirated using a syringe attached to the tube

Fluid Selection

Tap water for most cases

Normal saline for infants

Specific solutions (e.g., potassium permanganate) may be used for certain poisons

Residual Fluid

Leave a small amount of fluid to neutralize remaining poison

Contraindications

  • Corrosive Poisoning: Avoid except for carbolic acid (phenol) to prevent perforation
  • Convulsant Poisons: Risk of triggering seizures (e.g., strychnine)
  • Comatose Patients: High aspiration risk
  • Volatile Poisons/ Hydrocarbons: May cause aspiration pneumonitis

Alternative

Incorrect Options:

Organophosphate poisoning (Option A): Gastric lavage is recommended for organophosphate poisoning (e.g., insecticides) because it can effectively remove the poison from the stomach if performed early, particularly within 1 hour of ingestion. The risks of aspiration or complications are considered manageable in this case with proper techniques.

Ethanol poisoning (Option C): Gastric lavage is recommended in cases of ethanol poisoning if it is performed within 1 hour of ingestion. explanationHtml:
• The symptoms described—sweating, lacrimation, diarrhea, and bradycardia—are consistent with cholinergic toxicity, commonly caused by organophosphate or carbamate poisoning.
  • Atropine is the first-line treatment for cholinergic toxicity. It is a muscarinic receptor antagonist that counteracts the effects of excessive acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, reducing secretions, bradycardia, and other parasympathetic symptoms.

Symptoms

Muscarinic: Lethargy, Salivation, Diarrhea, Lacrimation, Urination, Miosis, Muscle weakness, Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia, Emesis (Mnemonic: DUMBBELLS)

Nicotinic: Muscle weakness, Fasciculation, Areflexia, Muscle paralysis

CNS: Headache, Tremor, Confusion, Slurred speech, Coma, Convulsion

Laboratory Diagnosis
  • RBC/True Cholinesterase (specific)
  • Plasma/Pseudocholinesterase (Most common)
    • Falls rapidly with organophosphorus poisoning
    • Inexpensive, sensitive)
  • Atropine test: If 2 mg of Atropine relieves symptoms, it confirms OP poisoning
  • P-nitro phenol test for confirmation.

Management
  • Resuscitative measures (Airway-Breathing-Circulation)
  • Decontamination
  • Gastric lavage with 1:5000 KMnO4
  • Activated charcoal
  • Atropine sulfate (2-4 mg IV every 10-15 minutes until atropinization)
  • Signs of atropinization: Heart rate>80 beats/min, pupils no longer pinpoint, clear chest on auscultation with no wheeze, systolic BP>80mmHg, Dry axillae
  • Oximes (Pralidoxime) to decrease muscarinic and CNS symptoms
    • removes phosphate group
    • reduces atropine requirement

Cause of Death

Respiratory Muscle Paralysis (RMP)

[[figure-1]]

Calcium gluconate (Option B): Used primarily for hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, or calcium channel blocker toxicity. It does not address cholinergic symptoms.

Pralidoxime (Option C): Pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivates acetylcholinesterase inhibited by organophosphates. It is used alongside atropine but is not the initial management step. Atropine is given first to stabilize the patient.

Obidoxime (Option D): Similar to pralidoxime, obidoxime is an oxime used to reactivate acetylcholinesterase. However, it is not the primary treatment for immediate symptom control.

• A "hooch tragedy" refers to incidents of poisoning caused by the consumption of illicit or adulterated alcohol.

  • Ingesting methanol leads to metabolic acidosis, blindness, and potentially fatal outcomes due to its toxic metabolites, formaldehyde and formic acid.

Phosphorus (Option A): Phosphorus poisoning typically occurs due to ingestion of rodenticides or fireworks, causing severe gastrointestinal and hepatic damage. It is not related to hooch tragedies.

Mercury (Option B): Mercury poisoning occurs due to exposure to mercury compounds, causing neurological and renal toxicity. It is unrelated to alcohol adulteration.

Explanation:

In plants like Aconitum (commonly known as aconite or monkshood), all parts of the plant, including the roots, leaves, and flowers, are toxic. The plant contains potent alkaloids such as aconitine, which can cause poisoning if ingested.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Species

Aconitum napellus, Aconitum ferox

Synonyms

Monk’s hood, mitha zaher, bish, wolf’s bane, women’s bane, devil’s helmet, or blue rocket

Source
  • All parts of the plant are poisonous (Option A)
  • Root and root tubers are the most potent (often mistaken for horseradish root)
  • Grown in Mountainous areas of the northern hemisphere. Eg. Sub Himalayan range (Option D ruled out)

Active Principles

Aconitine, pseudo-aconitine, indaconitine, picraconitine, aconine.

Mechanism of Action

Affects voltage-sensitive sodium channels, stimulates then paralyzes sensory nerves, secretory nerves, CNS, and myocardium.

Symptoms (by system)
  • GIT: Nausea, vomiting, salivation, abdominal pain, diarrhea, burning/tingling of mouth, tongue, throat, followed by numbness.
  • CVS: Hypotension, AV block, bradycardia, chest pain, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, slow/feeble pulse. (Option B ruled out)
  • CNS: Vertigo, restlessness, headache, giddiness.
  • MS: Muscle weakness, twitching, spasms.
  • RS: Slow, labored, shallow breathing.
  • Ocular: Alternating pupil dilation/contraction (hippus), diplopia, impaired vision.
  • Others: Subnormal temperature, cold skin, yellow-green vision, tinnitus, paralysis of facial muscles.
  • Death: Respiratory failure or ventricular fibrillation.

Fatal Dose

Root: 1-2 g

Treatment
  • No specific antidote.
  • Gastric lavage with tannic acid/activated charcoal.
  • Inotropic therapy for hypotension, atropine for bradycardia. (Option C ruled out)
  • Ventricular arrhythmia treated with amiodarone, flecainide; cardiopulmonary bypass for refractory cases.

Medico-legal Aspects
  • Ideal homicidal poison: cheap, easily available, small lethal dose, short fatal period, difficult to detect postmortem.
  • Accidental poisoning: mistaken for horseradish

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The primary cause of death in smoke inhalation is anemic hypoxia, which occurs due to the inability of hemoglobin to effectively transport oxygen to tissues. This condition can arise from carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, a common consequence of smoke inhalation. CO has a much higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, which leads to reduced oxygen delivery to vital organs, ultimately causing systemic hypoxia and potential organ failure.

Incorrect Options:

Histotoxic hypoxia (Option A) occurs when cells are unable to effectively use oxygen, often due to the presence of toxic substances, such as cyanide. While cyanide can be released during combustion, histotoxic hypoxia is not the primary cause of death in smoke inhalation. The main mechanism of death in smoke inhalation is related to the impaired ability of hemoglobin to carry oxygen, as seen in anemic hypoxia.

Ischemic hypoxia (Option B) results from inadequate blood flow to tissues, which can lead to a shortage of oxygen supply. In severe cases of smoke inhalation, respiratory failure could reduce oxygen perfusion to tissues, but this is not the primary cause of death in most cases of smoke inhalation. The main issue is the impaired oxygen binding by hemoglobin due to carbon monoxide (CO), leading to anemic hypoxia.

All of the above (Option D): While histotoxic hypoxia and ischemic hypoxia can be involved in some cases of smoke inhalation (especially if toxic gases like cyanide are present), anemic hypoxia is the primary cause of death in smoke inhalation due to the carbon monoxide (CO) binding to hemoglobin. Therefore, "All of the above" is not the correct answer.



Reference:
  1. Smoke Inhalation
  2. Smoke Inhalation Injury: Etiopathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management - PMC
  3. Hypoxia (Hypoxemia): Low Blood Oxygen Signs, Causes, Treatment

Yellow oleander, Digoxin and Yellow oleander, Physostigmine (Option C and D)

Origin

Mechanism of action
  • It is a potent central nervous system (CNS) stimulant that produces initial euphoria and increased energy, followed by depression as its effects wear off.

The image of the marking nut is Bhilawanol-Semecarpus Anacardium

Semecarpus Anacardium:

  • Abrus precatorius is used as an arrow poison and ideal cattle poison.

Semecarpus Anacardium:

  • Commonly known as the marking nut or bhilawanol (washermen use its juice to inscribe identification numbers on clothes).
  • Seeds:
    • Black, cone/heart-shaped with a rough projection at the base.
    • They have a thick pericarp that contains an acrid, brownish, oily juice that turns black upon exposure to air.

[[figure-1]]

  • Active principles: Semecarpol and Bhilawanol
  • Signs and Symptoms:
    • Skin exposure: Applying the juice can cause irritation, itching, and painful blisters filled with acrid serum. Eczematous eruptions resembling bruises may also occur, potentially evolving into ulcers with sloughing.
    • Constitutional symptoms include fever and painful micturition, often accompanied by brown-colored urine.
    • Oral ingestion: A large dose can cause blisters in the mouth and throat, severe gastrointestinal irritation, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension, cyanosis, loss of reflexes, delirium, coma, and potentially death.
    • Fatal dose: Approximately 5–10 g (5–8 seeds).
    • Fatal period: 12–24 hours.
  • Treatment:
    • Rinse the affected skin with soap and water.
    • Apply bland liniments.
    • Provide demulcent drinks and symptomatic treatment.
  • Medico-legal Aspects:
    • Criminal Use: The juice can be introduced vaginally as a form of punishment for infidelity or applied to the cervical os for illegal abortions.
    • Malingering: The juice can simulate conjunctivitis or falsely substantiate assault claims, as the lesions resemble bruises

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Atropine and neostigmine are not routinely used as primary treatment for krait bites.
  • While neostigmine may assist in reversing neurotoxic paralysis caused by snake venom (e.g., postsynaptic blockade in some bites), its role is secondary to antivenom therapy and ventilatory support.
  • Atropine is given to counteract bradycardia caused by neostigmine but is not specific to krait bites.

Treatment of snake bite:

First Aid: ‘ CARRY NO RIGHT ’

CARRY
  • Do not allow the victim to walk on their own, must be carried (in any form) to the hospital as soon as possible.

NO
  • No Suction
  • No Cautery
  • No Ligature
  • No Tourniquet

RIGHT
  • R: Reassure the patient
  • I: Immobilize the limb: by application of crepe bandages (Sutherland wraps)
  • GH: Get to the Hospital immediately
  • T: Tell history/symptoms

Pressure bandage
  • Used for immobilization of the limb by application of crepe bandage - known as Sutherland wraps.
  • Contraindicated in viper bites.
  • Ideal pressure: 50-70 mm Hg.

ASV
  • Mainstay of treatment.
  • Used only when signs of systemic poisoning are present
  • Polyvalent anti snake venom (PAV) used in India can neutralize (i) Cobra (ii) Krait (iii) Russel viper (iv) Saw-scaled viper bites.
  • Dose: 1-2 ml/kg (!0 vials) irrespective of sex/age.
  • Each vial: neutralizes 6-8 mg of snake venom
  • Test dose is not required/advised to be given before initiating ASV.
  • Ideally to be given within 4 hours of snake bite.
  • To be given until clinical improvement (in cobra bites)/ Clotting time becomes normal (in viper bites).

Adjuvant treatment
  • Neostigmine 1.5mg: for neuroparalytic symptoms (cobra bite).
  • Atropine 0.5mg: To antagonize muscarinic actions of Ach.
  • Surgical debridement and FFP may be required in Viper bites.


Incorrect Options:

Neostigmine and ventilatory support are used in treatment along with ASV (Option B): Neostigmine may help reverse neurotoxic effects (especially postsynaptic) when combined with ventilatory support. Anti-snake venom (ASV) remains the primary treatment.

ASV is the mainstay of treatment (Option C): Polyvalent ASV is the mainstay for treating bites from the "big four" venomous snakes in India (cobra, krait, Russell's viper, and saw-scaled viper).

Current ASV in India is not effective against humped pit viper (Option D): The polyvalent ASV available in India is ineffective against humped pit viper venom because it does not include antibodies specific to this species.

Explanation:

It has the ability to accumulate in bones over time, making it detectable even after the decomposition of soft tissues. Arsenic is a heavy metal, it replaces phosphorus and gets absorbed into the bones, where it may remain for years.

Postmortem findings of Arsenic Poisoning

External findings

Internal findings

  • Emaciation
  • Raindrop pigmentation
  • Keratosis
  • Alopecia

[[figure-1]]

  • Nasal septum ulceration.
  • Sunken eyeballs

  • Rigor mortis (sets in late and persists for a prolonged duration)
  • Reddening of stomach mucosa (red velvet or strawberry) due to gastrointestinal congestion.

[[figure-2]]

  • The inflammation and presence of “rice water” contents in the intestines.
  • Subendocardial haemorrhages in the heart.

[[figure-3]]

  • Fatty degeneration of the heart, liver, and kidneys.
  • Along with routine viscera and body fluids, the items preserved for chemical analysis are:
      • A piece of long bone (preferably femur)
      • A bunch of pulled scalp hair
      • A wedge of muscle
      • A small portion of skin (from the back of the trunk)

Carbon monoxide (Option B) is a gas that is produced during the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing materials. It is unlikely to be found in skeletonized remains since it is a volatile gas that dissipates quickly and does not accumulate in the body or bones.

Hydrogen sulphide (Option C) is a toxic gas that has a strong odor of rotten eggs. Similar to carbon monoxide, it is unlikely to be found in skeletonized remains as it is a volatile gas that dissipates rapidly and does not accumulate in the body or bones.

Phosphorus (Option D) is a chemical element that can be toxic in certain forms, such as white phosphorus. However, it is not typically found in skeletonized remains as it is highly reactive and tends to undergo chemical reactions or degradation over time.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A locked room with a running heat stove is a classic setup for carbon monoxide (CO) accumulation due to incomplete combustion of fuel. CO binds to hemoglobin with ~200–250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. This results in hypoxic injury and death.
  • CO poisoning often occurs in enclosed spaces with faulty heaters, stoves, or car exhaust.
  • Clinical features include headache, dizziness, cherry-red skin, confusion, and loss of consciousness. Death results from tissue hypoxia despite normal PaO₂.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated carboxyhemoglobin levels.

Treatment: Immediate removal from the source and administration of 100% oxygen or hyperbaric oxygen therapy in severe cases.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Organophosphate (OP) poisoning causes cholinergic overstimulation by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.

Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, used to treat the muscarinic symptoms of OP poisoning.

OPC poisoning:

Symptoms

Muscarinic: Lethargy, Salivation, Diarrhea, Lacrimation, Urination, Miosis, Muscle weakness, Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia, Emesis (Mnemonic: DUMBBELLS)

Nicotinic: Muscle weakness, Fasciculation, Areflexia, Muscle paralysis

CNS: Headache, Tremor, Confusion, Slurred speech, Coma, Convulsion

Laboratory Diagnosis
  • RBC/True Cholinesterase (specific)
  • Plasma/Pseudocholinesterase (Most common)
    • Falls rapidly with organophosphorus poisoning
    • Inexpensive, sensitive)
  • Atropine test: If 2 mg of Atropine relieves symptoms, it confirms OP poisoning
  • P-nitro phenol test for confirmation.

Management
  • Resuscitative measures (Airway-Breathing-Circulation)
  • Decontamination
  • Gastric lavage with 1:5000 KMnO4
  • Activated charcoal
  • Atropine sulfate (2-4 mg IV every 10-15 minutes until atropinization)
  • Signs of atropinization: Heart rate>80 beats/min, pupils no longer pinpoint, clear chest on auscultation with no wheeze, systolic BP>80mmHg, Dry axillae
  • Oximes (Pralidoxime) to decrease muscarinic and CNS symptoms
    • removes phosphate group
    • reduces atropine requirement

Cause of Death

Respiratory Muscle Paralysis (RMP)

[[figure-1]]

Option Explanation Seen after atropine?
Bradycardia Reversed by atropine (muscarinic blockade) Not seen
Muscle weakness Nicotinic effect; not reversed by atropine Seen
Diaphoresis Muscarinic effect; reversed by atropine Seen before, improves
Nasal discharge Muscarinic effect; reversed by atropine Seen before, improves

Muscle weakness (option B): Remains because atropine does not affect nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

Diaphoresis (option C): Caused by muscarinic stimulation → improves with atropine.

Nasal discharge (option D): Muscarinic effect → improves with atropine.

question: A patient came to the hospital with muscle weakness, diarrhea, and bradycardia. He was diagnosed with organophosphate poisoning for which atropine was administered. After atropine administration, which of the following changes are not seen?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Arsenic:

Aldrich-Mees lines (transverse white lines across the nails) and raindrop pigmentation (brownish discoloration) on the hands are characteristic signs of arsenic poisoning. Arsenic is known to cause these distinctive dermatological and nail changes. Arsenic interferes with the keratinization process in the nails, leading to the formation of Mees lines, and can cause pigmentary changes in the skin.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Thallium:

Thallium poisoning can cause symptoms like hair loss, peripheral neuropathy, and gastrointestinal issues, but it is not typically associated with Aldrich-Mees lines or raindrop pigmentation. Thallium poisoning does have its own set of diagnostic signs but these specific ones are not characteristic.

Option C - Cadmium:

Cadmium poisoning is associated with kidney damage and bone disease, not with Aldrich-Mees lines or raindrop pigmentation. Cadmium does not produce the same dermatological findings as arsenic.

Option D - Lead:

Lead poisoning is associated with basophilic stippling of red blood cells, but it does not typically present with Aldrich-Mees lines or raindrop pigmentation. Lead affects different body systems and has different clinical manifestations.

question: A 40-year-old female consumed a white-colored rodenticide powder and presents with a potassium level of 2.5 mEq/L. On examination, she has an irregular pulse and muscle paralysis. ECG shows multiple ventricular ectopics. What is the suspected poison?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Saturnism:

  • Saturnism, also known as chronic lead poisoning, can cause a variety of hematological abnormalities, including anemia, basophilic stippling, and the presence of nucleated red blood cells (RBCs) in the peripheral blood.

  • In severe cases, lead poisoning can also lead to bone marrow suppression, which can result in pancytopenia.

  • However, it is important to note that the hematological picture of lead poisoning can vary depending on the level and duration of exposure, as well as individual factors such as age and nutritional status.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Minamata disease: While it is possible that mercury toxicity may lead to some degree of hematological abnormalities, such as anemia, the typical hematological picture of Minamata disease does not include specific features that would clearly distinguish it from other causes of anemia.

Option C - Chronic iron toxicity: Chronic iron toxicity can lead to a hematological picture of microcytic hypochromic anemia, which is characterized by small red blood cells that contain insufficient hemoglobin. While this is a specific hematological feature that can be seen in chronic iron toxicity, it is not unique to this condition and can also occur in other forms of anemia.

Option D - Arsenic poisoning: Arsenic poisoning can lead to a variety of hematological abnormalities, including anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. The specific hematological picture may vary depending on the severity and duration of exposure. However, the presence of anemia alone is not specific enough to diagnose arsenic poisoning, as anemia can also occur in many other conditions.



Reference:

explanationHtml:

Explanation:

  • Hydrocarbons (such as gasoline, kerosene, or other petroleum products) are highly dangerous if aspirated into the lungs. They can cause severe chemical pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia, so gastric lavage is contraindicated in hydrocarbon poisoning.

Gastric Lavage in Poisoning Management

[[figure-1]]

  • Gastric lavage is a procedure to remove ingested poison by introducing and withdrawing fluids through an orogastric tube. Its effectiveness depends on timing, proper technique, and patient-specific considerations.

Timing and Effectiveness

  • Most effective within 1 hour of ingestion (Option A ruled out) (Gastric lavage may be considered because strychnine is a rapidly absorbed, highly toxic substance. However, the risk of seizures and subsequent aspiration is very high, so benzodiazepines must be administered first to control convulsions before attempting the procedure.)
  • Can be beneficial up to 4-6 hours in select cases
  • Beyond 6 hours, poison likely passes into the intestines, reducing lavage efficacy

Procedure Steps

Step

Details

Patient Positioning

Trendelenburg: Head down to prevent aspiration

Left lateral decubitus: Reduces chance of poison entering the duodenum

Tube Placement Confirmation

Inject air and listen for gastric bubbling sounds

Watch for coughing or bubbles (indicates misplacement in trachea)

Fluid Administration

Fluid is administered and aspirated using a syringe attached to the tube

Fluid Selection

Tap water for most cases

Normal saline for infants

Specific solutions (e.g., potassium permanganate) may be used for certain poisons

Residual Fluid

Leave a small amount of fluid to neutralize remaining poison

Contraindications

  • Corrosive Poisoning: Avoid except for carbolic acid (phenol) to prevent perforation
  • Convulsant Poisons: Risk of triggering seizures (e.g., strychnine)
  • Comatose Patients: High aspiration risk
  • Volatile Poisons/Hydrocarbons: May cause aspiration pneumonitis (Option C)
  • Risk of Hemorrhage/Perforation: Avoid if esophageal varices or recent surgery present
  • Additional Contraindications to Emetics
    • Severe heart or lung diseases
    • Advanced pregnancy
    • CNS depression or seizures

Complications

Complication

Details

Aspiration

Occurs in ~10% of cases. Risk of lung injury

Esophageal/Gastric Perforation

Can be life-threatening

Tube Misplacement

Misplaced into trachea, causing complications

Bleeding

Can occur with improper technique or pathology

Alternative

Description

Induce vomiting in conscious patients

Large water intake to dilute corrosive substances

Used for toxic foreign bodies or drug packets
